articles.title: Carney cites her award-winning book on encampments. She's eyeing his plan to end homelessness
articles.summary: One of Canada's leading authors on homelessness says the prime minister’s plan to end it within 10 years is an "ambitious goal" that has potential, but won't actually go all the way.

image.caption: Award-winning author Maggie Helwig stands outside her Toronto church as city workers clear an unhoused encampment at St. Stephen-in-the-Fields, where she serves as an Anglican priest. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics
One of Canada's leading authors on homelessness says the prime minister’s plan to end it within 10 years is an "ambitious goal" that has potential, but won't actually go all the way.
Author, Anglican priest Maggie Helwig says budget's signature pledge is ambitious — but won't go all the way
One of Canada's leading authors on homelessness says the prime minister's plan to end it is an "ambitious goal" that has potential, but won't actually go all the way.
Prime Minister Mark Carney introduced his government's second budget last week, which features a big headline promise: end homelessness in 10 years.

Governments sometimes tease big pledges in the run up to tabling a budget. That wasn't the case with this year's signature pledge, but there was an Easter egg that could have pointed to this new policy focus.
Earlier this year, Carney told the Globe and Mail that he was reading Encampment by Maggie Helwig, which won this year's Shaughnessy Cohen Prize for political writing.

Encampment tells the story of Helwig's activism and effort to keep her Toronto churchyard open to those in need. The award jury called the book "a necessary, on-the-ground view of Canada's homelessness crisis."
November's budget went on to propose a $11.2-billion cash injection to tackle homelessness, one of this year's largest line items.
Carney is not the first politician in Canada's history to set this target, but with Canadians facing an escalating affordability and housing availability crisis, the stakes are high.
Helwig gave her assessment of Carney's plan to CBC's chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton.

"I think that the commitments which have been made are serious commitments. They are constructive commitments. They are not at a scale which would end homelessness," Helwig said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live.
"If we are able to significantly reduce levels of homelessness, especially unsheltered homelessness, that's a big deal."
Helwig says Canada faces a very difficult situation with homelessness growing exponentially.

A national homelessness count in 2025 found that more than 65,000 people were homeless on a given night in Canada, a 59 per cent increase over five years. The share of unhoused people living in unsheltered locations, including encampments, had also increased from 23 per cent to 27 per cent.
What's needed in the Liberal plan?
Helwig's broad critique of the Liberals' proposal is that it should not overlook the straightforward need for more basic housing.
"I worry that there's a bit too much emphasis on mental health and addictions, as if those were the primary drivers of homelessness," she said.
Helwig says sometimes the issue is just needing a place someone can afford to live, since long-term homelessness itself is "fantastically destructive to people's mental and physical health."

Helwig helps move a resident's belongings as Toronto city workers prepare to clear an unhoused persons encampment at St. Stephen-in-the-Fields Church, in Toronto, on Oct. 16, 2025. (The Canadian Press)

Helwig points to Dunn House in Toronto as an example of a housing program where the focus is not exclusively on mental health and addiction, but which takes a more holistic picture of what people need when coming out of chronic homelessness.
It features direct access to doctors, nurses and a host of other health professionals with the goal of improving their health and alleviating pressure on hospitals.
"No one wants to move into the crazy house for the crazy people, right?" Helwig said, referring to projects that could over-emphasize mental health language.
Helwig says the reality is that some people do need intensive mental health support but it must be provided in a way that does not stigmatize individuals.
Influence on Carney
The day after making this pledge public, Carney cited Helwig during an announcement in Winnipeg.
While downplaying Barton's questions about whether she had a direct role in motivating Carney's new ambition, Helwig said it's nice to think her book may have contributed to it.

While listening to Carney speak publicly about the goal for the first time, Helwig noted Carney's use of language emphasizing Canada becoming a community that takes care of each other — a central theme to her book.
She said she's less concerned about whether the Liberals' plan will actually end all homelessness, compared to whether it will do good for the people who are sleeping on the streets right now.

"In a situation where we have seen so much stigmatizing language, so much demonizing language, so much emphasis on getting these people somewhere that's out of sight, to talk about this in terms of community and care, that in itself is actually quite important."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Mayson Maharaj is a producer for CBC's national television program Power & Politics and a writer for CBC's Parliament Hill bureau.

articles.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
articles.summary: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.

blocks.text: Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

articles.title: Polish activists face opposition as they make abortion more accessible
articles.summary: Abortion laws in Poland are very restrictive. Activists there have found a new way to help women wanting to terminate a pregnancy: the "Abortomat," a locker that dispenses abortion pills. But they…

image.caption: Polish activist Justyna Wydrzynska helps to operate the 'Abortomat,' a locker that allows women to access abortion pills swiftly and anonymouslyImage: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Women's rights activists in Poland have opened what they say is the world's first delivery locker supplying abortion pills in a country with one of Europe's most restrictive abortion laws.

Known as the "Abortomat," the locker is in a building opposite the Polish parliament, in what activists say is a clear message to politicians like Donald Tusk. The Polish prime minister pledged to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy before the 2023 parliamentary election, but his coalition has been unable to agree on a common position.
Only two European Union member states, Poland and Malta, do not allow abortion on request.
In Poland, abortion is only allowed when the pregnancy is the result of a crime — rape or incest — or when it endangers the health or life of the woman.
Pink lockers and PIN codes

Justyna Wydrzynska, an activist from a nonprofit organization called Abortion Dream Team, showed DW the "Abortomat" in a small room behind a tasseled portiere at Abotak, Poland's first abortion center.

blocks.caption: Abotak, Poland's first abortion center, is situated opposite the Polish parliament and houses the 'Abortomat'Image: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Inside, the pink lighting is subdued. Glitter tassels, baubles and spotlights make it feel a bit like a disco, she said.

The "Abortomat," which opened in late September, has 22 pink lockers. To open one, a woman receives a PIN code from the organization Women Help Women after completing a medical questionnaire, which is then checked by a doctor.
Parcel lockers have sprung up like mushrooms after rain in Poland in recent years. Even the smallest villages have them.
"When you walk around Poland, vending machines are everywhere. This is our culture. People in the US have Amazon, we have vending machines for everything," said Wydrzynska.
Convicted of helping a woman to have an abortion
Women in Poland who have an abortion are not criminalized. But anyone who helps them terminate a pregnancy risks up to three years in prison.
In 2023, Wydrzynska was the first activist to be convicted in Poland of helping a woman to have an abortion by sending her pills. The conviction was later overturned, and the court ordered a retrial.
'Abortomat': World's first abortion pill-dispensing locker in Poland
Inside each compartment at the "Abortomat" is a package that normally contains two drugs, mifepristone and misoprostol, usually taken up to the 14th week of pregnancy.

Because mifepristone is not registered in Poland, the drug must be ordered from abroad where it is legal. Information on how to do this is not easy to come by, which is where Abortion Dream Team and Abotak come in. They help women find information about accessing medication, which is sent from abroad by Women Help Women, or help them to travel abroad for a termination.
A 'complicated' legal situation
Wydrzynska said she believes the "Abortomat" does not break the law because it is a machine, not a person, that is delivering the pills, although she admits she is not sure.
Dr. Sabrina Mana-Walasek, a reproductive rights lawyer representing Wydrzynska, said the legal environment for abortion pills is "complicated."
She said that although mifepristone is not registered in Poland, it is registered in the European Union and, as EU citizens, Polish women can order it and take it.
"If a woman orders pills for herself and pays for them herself, it's not a crime," she said.
Opposition from Catholic groups
The ultra-Catholic legal group Ordo Iuris disagrees and has notified the prosecutor's office that the activists are committing a crime.

"In the case of an 'Abortomat,' the actions enabling a woman to have an abortion are theoretically performed by the woman herself using the device, but the reality is that this machine is operated by people — they send the code required to open the compartment containing abortion pills, they order and procure the pills, and they restock the compartments," said Katarzyna Gesiak, director of the Ordo Iuris Center for Medical Law and Bioethics.

blocks.caption: Comforting messages can be seen inside the Abotak center Image: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Wydrzynska said anti-abortion activists regularly demonstrate outside Abotak, using horns and loudspeakers to generate loud noise to annoy the center's residential neighbors and pressure the landlord to revoke their rental agreement.
At one demonstration, a woman holding an image of the Virgin Mary told DW she believes abortion "is the work of Satan."
"Abortion is evil, it's demonic, it's against the fifth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not kill,'" she said.
Support for women seeking an abortion

Earlier this year, Diana, a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman living in Warsaw, used abortion pills during her sixth week of pregnancy before the "Abortomat" started up. She got the pills using information provided by Abortion Dream Team.
Diana told DW that she has never wanted to have children.
"I was expecting something like a headache, stomachache, maybe vomiting, but I had nothing like that. It was just like a normal period. I didn't feel any pain. It was really easy for me," she said.
"I felt relief because I knew that it was the right choice for me. I knew that I can live my life," she added.

blocks.caption: Before receiving a PIN code for the locker, a woman first has to complete a medical questionnaire from the organization Women Help WomenImage: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Another Abortion Dream Team activist, Natalia Broniarczyk, said they help about 130 women daily in Poland. About 125 of these women use pills that cost about €75 ($83), while the remainder travel to a clinic abroad.
In contrast, just 851 abortions were performed in Polish hospitals last year.
Rising support for right-wing parties
Broniarczyk is concerned about the rising support for right-wing parties ahead of next year's parliamentary election, but she's also furious at the inactivity of liberals in Tusk's coalition.

"I'm mad at the liberals because for three years, they did nothing to protect us. They lost three years and now, when we're close to an election, they are fighting for our voices and respect. People are more progressive than politicians," she said.

After taking office in 2023, Tusk's coalition, which includes left-wing and conservative partners, were unable to agree a common position and their separate bills failed to obtain parliamentary approval in 2024.

blocks.caption: Natalia Broniarczyk believes Poland's president, Karol Nawrocki, will use his power of veto to block two bills recently passed by the country's parliament that would make abortion more accessibleImage: Adam Easton/DW

blocks.text: Afterwards, Tusk said abortion on request would not be possible during the current parliamentary term.
Two bills approved by parliament
In October, however, two bills were resubmitted to the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, and were narrowly approved.

One reinstates severe irreversible fetal defects as a justification for a legal termination. This justification had been ruled illegal by the Constitutional Court in 2020 when the previous right-wing Law and Justice (PiS)-led government was in power.
The 2020 ruling led to tens of thousands of people, mostly women, taking part in street protests in towns and cities across the country, some of the largest since communism fell in 1989.
Lawmakers also approved a bill partially decriminalizing anyone who helps a woman terminate her pregnancy.

According to the results of a recent poll conducted by SW Research for Onet.pl, almost 61% of respondents said they want the country's right-wing president, Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, to sign into law the bill on the fetal defect justification.
Nawrocki opposes abortion, and both Wydrzynska and Broniarczyk think he will use his power of veto to block the bills, preventing them from becoming law.

articles.title: Two killed in Leeds after car pursued by police crashes into another vehicle
articles.summary:
Four arrested after BMW collides with Volkswagen on Gelderd Road, with police appealing for witnesses

Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by…
articles.byline: Mark Brown North of England correspondent

blocks.text: Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police.
West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested after the crash in Leeds on Sunday and appealed for witnesses to come forward.

A force spokesperson said that at 12.44am a blue BMW 123D had failed to stop for a police vehicle in Gelderd Road, leading to a pursuit. The BMW then collided with a white Volkswagen Scirocco that was turning into Gelderd Road.

Police said the driver of the Volkswagen, a 22-year-old man from York, had been pronounced dead at the scene. A passenger in the same car, a 23-year-old woman from York, died in hospital a short time later. Neither has been formally named.

A 39-year-old man from Harrogate was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and driving while over the prescribed limit for cannabis in relation to the incident. He remains in custody.

Three other occupants of the BMW, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a 16-year-old girl, were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries that were not considered life-threatening. All three were arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

West Yorkshire police have referred themselves to the Independent Office for Police Conduct, which has declared an independent investigation. A spokesperson for the IOPC said: “We have started an independent investigation after a fatal road traffic collision in Leeds following a pursuit involving West Yorkshire police.

“After we were notified by West Yorkshire police, we declared an independent investigation at around 2.30am and sent investigators to the scene and police post-incident procedure to begin gathering evidence.
“Our inquiries are at a very early stage.”
The junction where the crash took place is surrounded by several car dealerships.

Pictures shared on social media overnight appeared to show an area around a segment of Gelderd Road cordoned off, with a fire engine and several police cars and ambulance vehicles in attendance. The pictures also appeared to show a dark car a short distance away from a very badly damaged white car just outside a used car dealership on Gelderd Road.
A cordon was still in place on Sunday morning with several officers in attendance, including a few inspecting the damaged cars. Drivers were advised to avoid the area.
Police appealed for witnesses and urged anyone with information or dashcam, mobile phone or CCTV footage to contact officers via 101 or online, quoting reference 13260649342.

articles.title: Gender-diverse Australian sailors barred from US submarines despite Aukus deal, documents reveal
articles.summary:
Defence briefing released under freedom of information laws shows ADF beholden to US directives when in training

  • Get our

blocks.text: Aukus is effectively forcing the Australian navy to comply with a US ban on transgender people in the military with gender-diverse navy recruits prevented from starting a career in nuclear submarines because they would not be safe training on US boats.
Internal Australian defence force documents show transgender and non-binary sailors and officers are explicitly banned from Australia’s nuclear submarine training program because of US policies..
An internal defence briefing, released under freedom of information laws, said while ADF policy on equality and inclusion was unchanged, “US government policy is different”.
“ADF personnel undertaking duty in the US (including training) are required to comply with US policy,” the briefing said.
“Consequently, transgender and nonbinary ADF personnel and ADF career applicants are currently unable to commence the SSN [nuclear-powered attack submarines] training pathway.”
Australia, without a nuclear submarine fleet of its own, has hundreds of sailors and officers training on US nuclear submarines and on US bases.

At a women in defence event in October, Rear Adm Tish van Stralen was asked how the defence force was “managing the recruitment of gender-diverse and LGBTQ+ Australians into the nuclear submarine pathway” given the US directive.
Van Stralen, one of the highest-ranking women in the Australian navy, said the ADF was a diverse and equal opportunity employer.
But she said potential recruits for the nuclear submarine program were told the ADF was “subject to policies and laws in other countries, so we have to be very mindful”.
“We also have an obligation, a duty of care to our people, so we do not want to put our people into any sort of harm’s way or anything that might adversely affect them.

“I’m working very closely with navy at the moment and with the submarine agency around the training opportunities because it would be very difficult for me to put a gender-diverse person into that training at the moment.”

Van Stralen said the navy would seek alternative career paths for gender-diverse recruits prohibited from the nuclear submarine program. She said the UK, Australia’s other Aukus partner, had “more liberal policies” and that training opportunities “may arise in the UK”.
“We don’t want to disadvantage people because of it but we are subject to the laws and policies of the US when we are in their country.”
after newsletter promotion
US moves came amid Aukus deal

The US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, last year issued a directive to his department “to eliminate all diversity, equity and inclusion offices and initiatives”. He also has sought to ban transgender personnel from joining the US military – repeatedly using offensive slurs in public statements – and ordered that transgender personnel be purged from the services.

Donald Trump signed an executive order in January 2025 – the first week of his second term as president – which banned transgender service personnel and said gender-diverse people were unfit to serve.
Announcing military cuts in September amid continued attacks on diversity, Hegseth declared that the US military would accept “no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals”.

Under the Aukus deal, it is proposed that Australia will buy three Virginia-class nuclear submarines from the US, beginning in 2032. In the lead-up to that, Australian sailors are training onboard US Virginia-class submarines and at US bases, while US-flagged nuclear submarines are porting in Australia.

Crewing Australia’s proposed nuclear submarine fleet is likely to prove one of the Aukus agreement’s most critical, sustained challenges. Virginia-class submarines have a complement of 135, more than double the crew for Australia’s diesel-electric Collins-class submarines.
Last week Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, said the Aukus timeline presented the country with a significant “training challenge”.
“We just need to be training more people and that’s what we’re doing,” Marles said at HMAS Stirling, the West Australian port through which US nuclear-powered submarines have been rotating.

The Australian defence department did not respond to questions from the Guardian about the impact of adhering to the US policy directive, including how many Australian service personnel have been prevented from undertaking nuclear submarine training.

The government’s nuclear-powered submarine workforce strategy urges defence to “proactively expand the talent pool through active inclusion of underrepresented groups, including women, First Nations Australians, regional communities, and individuals who may not traditionally see themselves in technical or defence-related careers”.

articles.title: Ethnic minority groups in Wales four times more likely to be target of police facial scans
articles.summary:
Exclusive: South Wales police figures show BAME people accounted for 24% of selected scans in 2025, despite being 7% of population

Ethnic minority people are four times more likely than…

blocks.text: Ethnic minority people are four times more likely than their white counterparts to be chosen for some police facial scans, according to official data, sparking warnings of racial bias.

Internal figures released by South Wales police revealed that 24% of people selected by police for facial recognition checks were from ethnic minorities, despite this group making up only 7% of the area’s total population.

The force polices Wales’s largest cities – Cardiff and Swansea – and has pioneered several versions of AI-enabled facial recognition technology. The latest figures relate to police officers capturing a person’s face with a smartphone and running the image through an algorithm called “Neoface” to match it against custody mugshots and other face databases. Most scans are made because people are suspected of crimes.

Civil liberties campaigners called the ethnicity figures “alarming”. The force said they raised “concerns about disproportionality” and that it was reviewing its approach. The data relates to a full year of use in 2025 and was obtained under the Freedom of Information Act and shared with the Guardian. Even when compared with arrest data for the police area, in which 11% of people arrested are from ethnic minorities, the face-scan figures appear disproportionate.

South Wales is one of the first UK constabularies to routinely use this “officer-initiated facial recognition” (OIFR) technology, which aims to identify suspects, wanted criminals and missing people who decline to give their details when challenged as well as people who are found unconscious, uncommunicative or dead. A similar system is being trialled by the Metropolitan police in London and has also been tested in Liverpool.

Critics have called facial recognition tools “Orwellian” and there have been repeated concerns about algorithmic bias putting ethnic minorities at greater risk of wrongful arrest. Last week, the police watchdog warned that innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, remained at risk of wrongful arrest if police treated inaccurate retrospective facial recognition data as evidence.

But advocates – including the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood – believe facial recognition is the biggest breakthrough for catching criminals since fingerprints and DNA matching. Other versions of the technology include live facial recognition cameras directed from marked vans and cameras fixed to lamp-posts, like those piloted in Croydon between October 2025 and March 2026, which led to 173 arrests, including of rape, kidnap and sexual assault suspects.

“This data shows that intrusive biometric tools are being used to disproportionately target minority communities,” said Jake Hurfurt, the head of research and investigations at Big Brother Watch, a civil liberties campaign that obtained the figures. “It is alarming that non-white people have been subject to face scans at a much higher rate than would be expected either by the region’s demography or the makeup of people arrested in the region.”
Aliya Mohammed, the chief executive of Race Equality First, a Cardiff-based anti-discrimination organisation, said the figures raised “serious concerns about racial disproportionality”.
“Facial recognition is not neutral because it uses AI,” she said. “If existing biases influence who is stopped and scanned, technology can reinforce and even amplify inequality.”

Alvi Choudhury, 26, who was arrested in February for a burglary in a city he had never visited after police face-scanning software confused him with another person of south Asian heritage on a custody database, said it was “very concerning” that ethnic minorities were being disproportionately scanned.
“The police are under pressure to solve crimes and they are over-reliant on these AI tools,” he said. “They shouldn’t be arresting people based on the AI tools alone.”
He remained worried AI systems were not trained on enough ethnic minority faces to ensure the number of false positives was no greater than for white people.

According to the data for 2025, South Wales police officers initiated face scans of 257 adults and 14 children, including two under-10s. More than half were suspected of a crime, being unlawfully at large or breaching bail conditions. The next most common reasons were because officers believed the person posed a risk of harm to themselves or others – such as stalkers or sex offenders. In about one in 10 cases, a scan was initiated for a suspected missing person while the technology was used to identify a dead person about once a fortnight.

In many of the cases, the scan failed to deliver a match or the subject agreed to share their identity. Where a match was made, arrests followed in 48% of cases and no further action resulted in a third of cases.

A spokesperson for South Wales police said: “We recognise the figures raise concerns about disproportionality. The number of OIFR searches remains relatively small, and the use of the technology is in its infancy. That said, each deployment is based on the individual circumstances that officers are dealing with at that time and is subject to supervisory and force-wide scrutiny.”

They said the force would “continue to review our approach through our established governance processes, which also include input from independent advisory groups and external scrutiny panels” and added: “Where opportunities for learning or improvement are identified, we will take appropriate action.”

Earlier this month, the Home Office announced a new facial recognition watchdog with the power to stop police forces using the technology if they fail to follow rules and new laws in the police reform bill, including a duty for the use of face scans to be intelligence-led and proportionate.

The Home Office said decisions on the operational use of facial recognition were matters for the police, but they must comply with equality, human rights and data protection laws and its use must be necessary, proportionate and fair.

articles.title: Cyprus, Slovakia, Slovenia join ASEAN Treaty of Amity and Cooperation
articles.summary: The Republic of Cyprus, the Slovak Republic, and the Republic of Slovenia have formally joined ASEAN"s Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia (TAC) on Saturday, November 14, 2026.

blocks.text: Published November 15, 2026 9:45pm
The Republic of Cyprus, the Slovak Republic, and the Republic of Slovenia have formally joined ASEAN’s Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia (TAC) on Saturday, November 14, 2026.

Cyprus Minister Evanthia Tsolaki, Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár, and Slovenian Foreign Minister Tone Kajzer signed and deposited their respective instruments of accession to the treaty ahead of the 49th ASEAN Summit opening ceremony.
Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro likened the accession to the Filipino concept of “pakikiisa,” or solidarity, with the ASEAN bloc.
She underscored the importance of supporting the pact amid persistent tensions in parts of the region.

“Each accession is more than just an expression of support for the TAC and ASEAN. This is what we call in Tagalog, pakikiisa, a decision to join in a common undertaking of peace and commitment towards cooperation,” Lazaro said.

“This is particularly important to the current geopolitical environment we face today, where escalating tensions, strategic competition, rivalries, and protracted conflicts continue to challenge the foundations of global peace and stability,” she added.

Lazaro said the expansion of signatories to the treaty reaffirms the enduring relevance and indispensable role of the TAC in upholding regional and global peace through mutual respect, peaceful settlement of disputes, non-interference, and effective cooperation.
The TAC is ASEAN’s foundational peace and security treaty, setting out the principles of peaceful coexistence, mutual respect, and cooperation among its high contracting parties.
Earlier this year, Poland also formally acceded to the pact as the regional bloc commemorates the 50th anniversary of the treaty's signing.

The three newly acceded countries noted that their entry into the treaty reflects a strong commitment to mutual respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the peaceful settlement of disputes in accordance with international law.

Slovak Foreign Minister Blanár, who attended the official opening of the Slovak Embassy in the Philippines earlier this week, expressed optimism that Slovakia's accession to the TAC would foster stronger ties with ASEAN and bring greater benefits to the peoples of all member states.

“We are convinced that closer cooperation between Slovakia and ASEAN (22:50) will bring tangible benefits to our peoples and contribute to peace, stability, and prosperity in our region. Today, signature reflects that ambition,” Blanár said.
The 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits will be held from November 16 to 18 at the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC) in Pasay City. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
articles.summary: It marks the second attack on the country in three days and comes as the US and Iran remain locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz.

blocks.text: Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.
The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.
Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".
It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.

The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.

Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.
As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.

Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."

In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."
Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.
The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage.
Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

articles.title: Poundland pins rescue hopes on Yorkshire Tea, Pot Noodle and Gloria Gaynor
articles.summary:
Chain restocks stores in operation named after singer of I will Survive after US owners release funds

Poundland’s under-fire US owners have released funds to help the stricken discount chain…

blocks.text: Poundland’s under-fire US owners have released funds to help the stricken discount chain restock shelves temporarily, keeping hopes of a rescue deal alive in the run-up to crunch talks with the government.
In an emergency resupply effort codenamed “Operation Gloria” by senior Poundland staff, about 16m grocery items were dispatched to 600 shops in the UK and Ireland over the weekend.

The name comes from the Gloria Gaynor song I Will Survive, which soundtracked a defiant video posted on social media by Poundland showing pallets of Yorkshire Tea and Pot Noodles making their way from depots to the shelves.
It came after Gordon Brothers, the US investors who MPs have accused of “predatory capitalism”, agreed to unlock £21m of £50m that it had been accused of endangering the business by withholding.

blocks.caption: Poundland staff have named the restocking operation after Gloria Gaynor, the singer of the 1970s hit I Will Survive.  Photograph: BBC

blocks.text: The money will provide breathing space while rescue talks continue, ensuring that suppliers continue sending goods to branches during the crucial pre-Christmas trading period.
Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the end of last month, throwing the fate of its 12,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers into uncertainty.
Last week the chain won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors, giving it until 26 November to find a buyer.
The company and Gordon Brothers are now heading for a frantic period of talks with potential buyers and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds.

Discussions could be soured by allegations – denied by Gordon Brothers – that the US investment group is more interested in protecting its own interests by breaking up the business despite signs of a dramatic improvement in its trading performance.
Gordon Brothers bought Poundland from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1 and claims to have rescued the company from collapse when nobody else would.
However, the US business has faced criticism from MPs, who have accused it of extracting millions of pounds as Poundland found itself on a knife-edge.
Liam Byrne, the chair of the business select committee, has likened Gordon Brothers to “the wolf of Wall Street, on the British high street”.
Documents provided to MPs showed the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures since acquiring Poundland.
Gordon Brothers has denied freezing any funds that should have been available to Poundland and pointed to loans that it has provided to prop up the company.
after newsletter promotion
Reynolds plans to meet Poundland and Gordon Brothers before the deadline to stave off administration runs out, according to a report by Sky News.
He and Andy Burnham have expressed concerns about Gordon Brothers’ conduct, with the prime minister asking why the US company has yet to accept an offer for a business that employs 11,000 people.
Poundland has said it is in discussions with three potential buyers.
Bids from the investment groups Xyra Group Holdings and Innovest are understood to have relatively little chance of success.
Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish company, is Poundland’s preferred bidder but progress has stalled over the repayment terms of a loan from Gordon Brothers.
A number of high-street retailers, including Tesco, are understood to be eyeing up some of Poundland’s shops.
The Guardian has approached Gordon Brothers, the business department and Poundland for comment.

articles.title: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
articles.summary: Han Won-seok, 34, confessed to using a hidden camera and AI to get a near-perfect mark on the significant test.

blocks.text: A candidate who came first in South Korea's certified tax accountancy exam has admitted cheating by using a miniature camera, mobile phone and AI tools.
Han Won-seok confessed in a video on the YouTube account of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho, adding that he had confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and offered details on how he cheated.
The 34-year-old scored 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, getting just one of 160 questions wrong, which initially raised suspicions and sparked online speculation.
Standardised national tests play an outsized role in career trajectories for South Koreans, making their results - and efforts to unduly inflate those results - of great importance.
"I cheated in both the first and second rounds of the tax account exam by using electronic devices and generative AI," Han said in the video published on Sunday.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating."

When accusations he had cheated first began to surface, Han had denied any wrongdoing - but said he had changed his mind after thinking about the feelings of the candidate who had come second in the exam.
He went on to apologise to the other entrants who had passed the tests fairly.
"It seems that because of me, other successful candidates are being suspected," he suggested.
The Ministry of Employment and Labour and the Human Resources Development Service held an emergency meeting after Han admitted cheating.
The South Korean president's policy chief Ha Jun-kyung said new measures would be introduced to prevent cheating and warned "past crimes" would be "tracked down and apprehended to the very end".
Those found to have used AI to cheat in the tax accountancy exam will have their qualification revoked and will be banned from retaking the test for five years, the government said.
The scandal comes just days before the east Asian nation's annual college entrance exam, a crucial hurdle for students.

articles.title: Cold and health alerts issued for Scotland and northern England as snow and ice expected
articles.summary:
UKHSA warns of health impact on those vulnerable to cold and urges people to check in with neighbours

Cold weather warnings have been issued for parts of the UK, as alerts for the risk to…

blocks.text: Cold weather warnings have been issued for parts of the UK, as alerts for the risk to health services are due to begin on Sunday evening.
The Met Office issued yellow weather warnings for ice for central and eastern Scotland from 6pm on Sunday evening until 10am on Monday.
People should be vigilant as they travel due to the risk from slipping on footpaths in icy conditions, it added.

It comes as the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) issued yellow cold health alerts for north-west and north-east England and for Yorkshire and the Humber about the impact of the cold snap on health services.
A previous warning for the West Midlands has been dropped.
They will come into force at 9pm on Sunday and run until Thursday morning.

The UKHSA alerts mean the weather is “likely to have minor impacts on health and social care services”, including an increased use of healthcare services and a greater risk to life for vulnerable people, the agency said.
Suffolk had the lowest temperature in the UK overnight into Sunday, with -4.5c recorded at Santon Downham.
The Met Office said snow could fall on hills in northern England and Scotland in the coming days.
after newsletter promotion
Dan Stroud, the senior operational meteorologist at the Met Office, said the cold weather was caused by northerly winds and longer nights.
Further weather warnings could be issued early in the week, the Met Office indicated. The weather will become briefly milder in midweek before returning to cold as the weekend approaches.
Stroud said: “The weather does try and settle down a little later in the period, with high pressure trying to build in from the middle of the week onwards from the north.
“So it will be turning brighter, but still plenty of showers in the mix. It will remain cold in the north, with temperatures remaining near average in the south.”
He added: “There will be a cold, widespread frost in the north on Friday, with daytime temperatures below normal, in single digits.”
Paul Coleman, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said: “This is the latest cold health alert of the season, and we can expect more as we move further into winter.

“Cold weather can have a serious impact on the health of some people, including those aged 65 and over and those with pre-existing health conditions, so it is vital to check in on friends, family and neighbours who are most vulnerable.”
Coleman added that people should try to heat the rooms they use the most, if possible, and dress warmly during colder spells.

articles.title: ‘Shameless venality’: how a flurry of lawsuits has thwarted Trump’s self-enrichment schemes
articles.summary:
Courts have issued stinging rebukes to president’s ‘blatant’ financial ploys as pro-democracy groups defend ‘government of laws, not of men’ pillar

Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys…

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s legal and political ploys to increase his wealth and boost Republican electoral prospects have fueled lawsuits by non-partisan groups, prompting federal judges to issue stinging rejections to some of the president’s schemes.

Several lawsuits were filed in 2026 against Trump’s schemes to benefit his bottom line by reducing potential tax liabilities, boosting his Truth Social platform financially by offering big investors early access to his posts, and helping Republicans by using federal funds to pay for highly partisan ads touting Trump’s record in the run-up to the midterm elections, in which Republicans suffered a heavy defeat.
The major lawsuits against Trump’s financial ploys have been the handiwork of several nonpartisan groups including Democracy Defenders Fund and the Campaign Legal Center.

In response, judges in Florida and New York used strong language to condemn and help nullify some of Trump’s financial stratagems. Florida judge Kathleen Williams castigated a Trump scheme backed by the justice department to settle a $10bn lawsuit he filed against the Internal Revenue Service over an old leak of his tax information to the New York Times.

Williams ruled that the Trump backed deal to set up a $1.8bn slush fund to pay alleged victims of political persecutions under Joe Biden and giving him immunity from IRS audits before May 2026 was “premised on deception” and a “fraud against the court”.

In a separate legal blow to Trump in the closing weeks of the campaign, the president was rebuked by a federal judge in New York, for channeling $20m of public funds to run ads touting his administration’s achievements. The ads were widely attacked as campaign ads and propaganda.
Former judges and ex-DoJ lawyers say that he Trump moves to boost his bottom line and political drives with backing from DoJ lawyers exemplify various kinds of Trump “corruption”.

Stacey Young, a former DoJ lawyer who set up Justice Connection last year as a network to defend the justice department workforce and the rule of law, told the Guardian: “The justice department’s leadership believes it has one chief client: President Trump. They have allowed him to use the department to protect his financial interests, punish his enemies, and reward his friends.
“Thanks to the efforts of some of the country’s best litigators, the people of the United States are pushing back and standing up for the ideal that we remain a government of laws, not of men.”

Further, retired federal appeals court judge J Michael Luttig said: “The courts have recently begun to strike down Trump’s countless schemes of blatant and shameless venality and corruption in the forms of self-enrichment, bribery, and extortion. That is the through-line of these three cases and the numerous other cases to come.”
For Luttig, the court rebuffs are part of a broader trend of federal courts also rejecting as unconstitutional major presidential initiatives including tariffs and birthright citizenship.

Luttig’s analysis was underscored by a July lawsuit filed by Democracy Defenders Fund and a coalition of 35 ex-judges, including Luttig, to kill a key piece of Trump’s proposed settlement of his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS by establishing a $1.8bn fund to pay alleged victims of political persecution that could have helped some January 6 Capitol rioters.

The DoJ dropped the slush-fund idea after Williams ruling and some political blowback by Congress. But despite Williams’s legal objections and sharp criticism from Democratic senators, including Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, a provision is still in effect providing immunity to Trump, his family and the Trump Organization from investigations and prosecutions of past tax matters by the IRS as compensation over a leak of his tax returns.

In her ruling, Williams charged that the plaintiffs initiated the lawsuit “for an improper purpose – to gain the imprimatur of judicial legitimacy for a ‘settlement’ that had no viable basis in law or fact”.

Williams’s scathing opinion in mid-July noted that Trump was on both sides of the issue and that the court itself was perhaps “the victim of fraud”. Williams concluded that the plaintiffs had acted in bad faith by “collusively filing a lawsuit with claims subject to multiple dispositive defenses solely to provide cover for a collusive settlement”.

Citing language from an earlier ruling, Williams said “this case is part of Mr Trump’s pattern of misusing the courts to serve political purposes”. In summary, Williams wrote, acidly, that the plaintiffs “pursued this lawsuit in bad faith for the improper purpose of dishonestly advancing a political narrative”.

Trump’s lawyers in late July said they would appeal the Williams order. In late September, a federal appeals court for the 11th circuit rejected a request from Trump and his lawyers to immediately lift sanctions that Williams imposed in response to the settlement Trump and the DoJ backed over the leak of his tax returns.

In its ruling, the appeals court denied a request by two Trump lawyers, Alejandro Brito and Daniel Epstein, to pause sanctions against them over their handling of his $10bn lawsuit against the IRS. The court ruled the lawyers had not demonstrated they would succeed in challenging finding that they acted in bad faith.

In another legal blow for Trump, two restraining orders were issued in October by district judge Jennifer Rochon in New York to stop his use of public funds for financing campaign style ads after Campaign Legal Center Action representing Common Cause, along with Public Integrity Project Action and Democracy Forward sued.
In her second emergency order on 30 October, Judge Rochon ruled that three ads could no longer run using government funds on Instagram and two other sites since they were “purely partisan” .

One of the ads echoed Trump’s dubious claim that if Republicans maintained control of Congress, all Americans would receive $5,000. The three ads Rochon ordered removed were headlined “$5,000 to Americans” the “Cost of Socialism” and “Every Democrat Voted against No Tax on Tips”.
Shortly before Rochon’s first ruling, Trump in a Truth Social post on 5 October defended using government funds for the ads and blithely stated that tapping public funds was “rather standard”.

But with growing criticism, including from some Republicans, Trump announced he would pay for them himself from his political fundraising operation. The justice department also tried to forestall the first restraining order by asserting that “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow”.

Renata O’Donnell, a senior legal counsel with Campaign Legal Center who worked on the case, told the Guardian: “The Department of Homeland Security used $20m in taxpayer dollars to pay a private ad agency for airtime for government-created propaganda. This is blatantly illegal.”

O’Donnell added: “In direct violation of the law, White House staff, whose salaries are paid with taxpayer dollars, were creating propaganda, including ads that promised people $5,000 to vote Republican.”

In another pending legal battle that courts have yet to rule on, Democracy Defenders Fund filed a lawsuit with the San Francisco city attorney, the Washington Litigation Group and Platkin LLP to block a Trump financial gambit to offer special early access to his Truth Social posts to users who pay a fee as high as $100,000 per month to the parent company of Truth Social.
The lawsuit was filed in mid-September against Trump Media and Technology Group, which operates and owns Truth Social.

San Francisco city attorney David Chiu asked the San Francisco superior court to bar Trump Media from offering its new service, dubbed “Trump API”, or a similar one, plus provide monetary damages for violating the public trust and the state’s unfair competition law.

“Trump Media created a marketplace that enables insider trading, which Trump directly profits from,” Chiu said in a statement. “This scheme turns the public trust into private profit. It is corruption, plain and simple.”

A Trump Media spokesperson ridiculed the lawsuit when it was filed, charging that “the people of California should outsource their future lawsuits to AI chatbots who, unlike the leftwing activists masquerading as attorneys who filed this lawsuit, will grasp the basic distinction between public and nonpublic information”.

David Ogden, a senior counsel with DDF who has worked on the case, noted that “Congress made clear that the president, like any public servant, shouldn’t be permitted to profiteer off of special access to government information. It’s a violation of the public trust and it’s important that it be stopped.”

In the eyes of Barbara McQuade, former US attorney for eastern Michigan, who now teaches law at the University of Michigan, the different court rulings against Trump’s financial ploys reveal his penchant for “personal enrichment” and political ploys during his presidency.

“It seems that Trump has no shame about using his office for personal enrichment. We can’t count on his own conscience, ethics or advisers to check his worst instincts, but the courts have seen through his various schemes, from his slush fund to his use of taxpayer funds for political ads.”

articles.title: We tested 6 popular apps to see what data they collect and share: CBC's Marketplace Cheat Sheet
articles.summary: The CBC's Marketplace rounds up the consumer and health news you need from the week.

image.caption: Marketplace tested six of the most popular Android and iOS apps in Canada – Tim Hortons, PC Optimum, Weather Network, Facebook, Amazon and YouTube – to find out what data they collect and where it’s shared. (CBC)

blocks.text: Miss something this week? Don't panic. The CBC's Marketplace rounds up the consumer and health news you need.
Want this in your inbox? Get the Marketplace newsletter every Friday.
We tested 6 popular apps to see what data they collect and share. Here's what we found
(CBC)
Whether you are buying a coffee, groceries, checking the weather or unwinding with an online video, there's a free mobile app for just about everything.
But a Marketplace investigation shows the cost of this convenience is your privacy — and the data you're sharing goes far beyond what you might realize.
Marketplace tested six of the most popular Android and iOS apps in Canada to find out what data they collect and where it goes.

To do so, Joel Reardon, an associate professor in the department of computer science, and his team at the University of Calgary scanned the network traffic of the apps on an Android device. Privo, an organization that evaluates apps to ensure they comply with U.S. child privacy laws, also did a scan of the apps on iOS, Apple's operating system.
In their user policies, the apps we tested explicitly disclose they collect or share certain data and that when you use the app, you accept their terms.
But Reardon and Celeste Rollason, an independent analyst who used to work with Privo, are concerned some apps collect more than they need and are sharing what they learn with others around the world.
That data ranges from your name and email address to your exact whereabouts.
"To me, this is not the internet we wanted. This is not the internet we deserve. It's turned into a monstrous data collection surveillance system," Reardon said.
To find out which apps we tested and what we found, read our full investigation from Bobby Hristova, Kathleen Coughlin and Rosa Marchitelli.
LinkedIn, Monster take down over 1,000 fake job postings after CBC investigation
Exposing who’s behind fake job ads online

More than 1,500 misleading job postings — offering remote work, no experience needed — have been taken down from LinkedIn and Monster after a CBC News visual investigation revealed the listings funnelled unsuspecting applicants to a multi-level marketing (MLM) company that asked for money.

CBC News connected a network of travel-related pages posting suspicious jobs — positions like "Work From Home Travel Planner and Virtual Customer Support Representative" — to a U.S.-based MLM called Evolution Travel. Some of the roles promised to pay up to $75,000 US per year.
In reality, there was no job and no salary.

Applicants were quickly directed to join virtual information sessions, where they were asked to pay hundreds of dollars up front, followed by a monthly subscription fee. The program promised to teach members how to make money from booking travel as an independent agent and recruiting others into the program, taking a cut of their commissions.
The companies went by names like Wanderwell Collective, Professional Travel Hub, Remote-Careers, Sky Land & Ocean Travel and Sunkissed Getaways.
The job postings made no mention of Evolution Travel or sign-up fees.

"This is disgusting," said Jay Jones, a Chicago-based job listing investigator who CBC shared its findings with. "They catch you with the lure of the fake job. The money is great, [successful applicants] get to stay at home. You have to pay to get work — that's not how work works."
Misleading job postings — including ones that require payment or lead to MLMs — are strictly prohibited on platforms like LinkedIn and other job sites.

A representative from Evolution Travel who only identified themselves by their title, chief operating officer, told CBC News they have consistently told their independent agents not to post job ads on any platforms.
Read the full investigation from the CBC's Eric Szeto, Courteney Dorrington, Jordan Pearson and Ivan Angelovski.
Worst of beef price hikes may be over, but don't expect cheaper steak anytime soon

Beef is cut at Ben's Quality Meats, a processing facility in Picture Butte, Alta. Canada's cattle herd is beginning to recover after years of declining numbers but experts say high production costs will keep beef prices elevated. (Monty Kruger/CBC)
After years of soaring beef prices, Canadians may finally be getting a break from steep price increases when buying their favourite cut of steak or roast at the grocery store.
Beef prices rose 8.7 per cent in September compared with a year earlier and have climbed 55.5 per cent over the past five years, according to Statistics Canada.
Prices remain at record highs, but industry experts say there are signs of stability, with grocery store price tags remaining relatively flat for much of 2026.
"The worst of the price jumps I would say are over," said Brenna Grant, executive director of Calgary-based beef statistics firm Canfax.

articles.title: PH: South China Sea Code of Conduct 80% done, to be completed at ASEAN 2027
articles.summary: Under the Philippines" ASEAN chairmanship this year, negotiations on the South China Sea Code of Conduct have progressed to 80% completion, leaving its finalization to Singapore.

blocks.text: Published November 15, 2026 8:41pm

Under the Philippines’ ASEAN chairmanship this year, negotiations on the South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) were nearly completed, leaving its finalization to Singapore, which will assume the chairmanship next year.

During a press briefing on Sunday, Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Secretary Tess Lazaro reiterated that the COC is 80% done, but added that it failed to reach completion under the country’s chairmanship due to time constraints in the negotiations.

“Negotiations are negotiations are negotiations. In other words, the 10 ASEAN countries plus China have also, of course, different views on how things are. So that is the reason why it was not really—I think there was not enough time,” she said.
“If we were given probably another five to six months, I think we can finish that,” she added.

In 2025, ASEAN member states and China agreed to conclude a COC on the South China Sea by 2026, with President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. likewise eyeing the completion of the pact during the Philippines' chairmanship.
Malacañang, meanwhile, earlier expressed hope that the COC would be signed before the Philippines' ASEAN chairmanship ends.

The proposed code seeks to establish rules to prevent disputes in the South China Sea from escalating and developing into a major armed conflict that could involve the United States, a Philippine ally, and other countries in the region.
The DFA said the Philippines still views the 80% milestone in drafting the code as an achievement, noting how far talks have come since Manila took over shepherding the negotiations.

“Sinabi ko nga [As I said], 80%, actually, it's even increasing as discussions continue. But I have to emphasize that it is one already of the achievements of the Philippines as chair, because what was the COC before we shepherded it, it was only about 50% perhaps,” Lazaro said.

“But to go to 80% and even moving, then there's a little bit. Konti na lang ang pag-uusapan nila sa [They will only have a little more left to discuss in] Singapore. But indeed, this Code of Conduct is really something that we can be proud of,” she added.
The Philippines is hosting this year's ASEAN Summit and is expected to turn over its chairmanship to Singapore. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: ASEAN offers Myanmar's sidelined leaders a path back to summits, but says restrictions will stay until there is meaningful progress on its peace plan
articles.summary: Southeast Asian leaders have agreed to engage Myanmar in stages after years of excluding its leaders from high-level meetings. The bloc says Myanmar could regain full representation if it makes…

image.caption: ASEAN leaders said Myanmar could gradually return to high-level meetings if it makes progress on the bloc's peace plan Image: Shunpei Takeuchi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Southeast Asian leaders agreed on Sunday to engage Myanmar's government in stages, while making its return to high-level meetings conditional on progress on a regional peace plan.
Myanmar remains a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but its political leaders have been barred from summits and foreign ministers' meetings since October 2021.
The military seized power that year, overthrowing the elected government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi and triggering a civil war that continues today.
What did ASEAN agree on Myanmar?
In a joint statement, the leaders called for "a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground.”

They said ASEAN could gradually restore Myanmar's full political representation if it makes "sustained and concrete progress” on the bloc's five-point peace plan. The plan has yielded little since it was agreed on in 2021, and fighting continues between the military and pro-democracy and ethnic armed groups.

"What more can we do for Myanmar?” Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. asked at the leaders' retreat in Manila. He urged the bloc to find practical ways to advance the peace plan and support an inclusive process led by Myanmar.
Thailand-Myanmar border clinic helps people fleeing war
Thailand has pushed for closer engagement since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing took office as civilian president this year following elections that monitors dismissed as a sham.
What else is on the agenda in Manila?

Leaders are also discussing trade, regional security and ways to share fuel supplies to cope with disruptions caused by the war in Iran. Australia and the Philippines signed a defense agreement on Sunday, while Canada and the Philippines announced on Saturday that they had concluded free trade negotiations.

A proposed code of conduct for the South China Sea remains unresolved. Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro said negotiations between ASEAN and China were 80% complete, but diplomats told AFP a deal was unlikely in Manila. Chinese Premier Li Qiang is representing Beijing at the summit.
What is Trump expected to do in Manila?

US President Donald Trump is expected to arrive on Tuesday, toward the end of the summit, and meet the leaders of India, Japan and Australia, the other members of the Quad. The meeting is expected to precede talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen on Thursday.
Activists plan to march against Trump's visit on Tuesday. Their protest is aimed in part at a US-backed industrial project north of Manila that they say could displace Indigenous families.
The Philippines hands the rotating ASEAN chair to Singapore next year, with Thailand due to take over in 2028.
