articles.title: Trump administration planning to reimburse doctors treating vaccine ‘injury’
articles.summary:
Experts warn that sweeping changes elevate health secretary RFK Jr’s anti-vaccine agenda and personal profit

The Trump administration is finalizing a

blocks.text: The Trump administration is finalizing a rule to reimburse doctors who diagnose, treat and counsel patients with side effects from vaccines in what experts believe is an attempt to undermine trust in vaccines and to create an evidence base on their purported risks.

Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), also announced the creation of a vaccine “injury” research center at the National Institutes of Health and has sought to reshape the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) – actions that point to Kennedy’s longtime activism against vaccination as well as the profits he and his network have made from vaccine lawsuits.
Kennedy and his allies have also profited from growing misinformation peddled through books, paid speaking events and the supplement industry.

“I do think he’s a real ideologue – he really believes in this,” said Dorit Reiss, professor of law at UC Law San Francisco. But Kennedy and his allies are likely “very happy to make money doing it”, she said.

Peter Hotez, professor and dean of Baylor College of Medicine’s National School of Tropical Medicine, agreed, saying Kennedy’s actions are likely a combination of “being an ideological zealot and making money either for himself or for his associates”.
Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, said the department “categorically reject claims that Secretary Kennedy is pursuing personal gain or seeking to dismantle American medicine”.

Prior to his confirmation hearing in January 2025, Kennedy disclosed $2.5m in income from referrals for vaccine-related lawsuits. In the hearing, Kennedy would not commit to forgoing compensation from vaccine lawsuits after he leaves office. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, listed several ways in which Kennedy’s actions, some of which have now happened, could influence future litigation.

“Kennedy can kill off access to vaccines and make millions of dollars while he does it,” Warren said at the hearing. “Kids might die. But Robert Kennedy can keep cashing in.” She pointed to Kennedy’s involvement in litigation against Merck for its HPV vaccine – lawsuits that were settled for more than $50m in June 2026. After the confirmation hearing, Kennedy said his son would receive the money, expected to be 10% of the total; it’s unclear if he did.
“For most of us, money going to our children isn’t exactly money not going to us,” Reiss said. “There’s a dozen ways he and his family could benefit” from Kennedy’s actions, she added.

Kennedy has long profited from his anti-vaccine misinformation. Tony Lyons, Kennedy’s publisher and a central figure in the constellation of Maha political organizations, reportedly paid Kennedy $4m in book advances over the past year. The publisher also paid Kennedy $451,000 in consulting fees before he became HHS secretary. That’s on top of other book sales and paid speaking engagements over the years. Kennedy also earned $326,000 for the 15 weeks he served as chairman of Children’s Health Defense in 2023 – more than half of his $510,000 salary in 2022.
More recently, he received free flights and trips on a yacht from a former donor to his presidential campaign, who is now under investigation by the Senate for the gifts totaling some $250,000.
As HHS secretary, Kennedy has also loosened regulations on peptides, a booming part of the largely unregulated wellness industry.

“I think he’s doing what everyone knew he was going to do,” said Hotez. Kennedy, before and during his tenure as leader of HHS, has been “chipping away at public confidence in vaccines and immunizations in favor of products that can be sold by the wellness industry”, he added.

Aaron Siri, Kennedy’s former lawyer who represents people who say they have experienced severe side effects, has advocated for changing all vaccines to “shared clinical decision-making”. If those changes took place, Siri could argue that the vaccines are not covered under the VICP and therefore open to litigation.
“A lot of what he is doing is geared toward setting up a more profitable litigation atmosphere,” Reiss said.

Siri did not respond to the Guardian’s question about profiting from litigation, but instead argued that “if vaccines are as ‘safe’ as touted by the government, then there should be no need for immunity to liability and, likewise, there should be very few, if any, successful cases”.
The most common claim to VICP – making up more than half – has to do with where the vaccine is administered, not the vaccines themselves.

The VICP was established in 1986 in order to expedite compensation for anyone who experienced adverse side effects from vaccines. There are real costs to undermining the program, Reiss said. It’s very rare for people to develop severe side effects after vaccination, but when they do, they should be compensated, she said. But if false claims about vaccine harms proliferate, they will obscure those with legitimate claims.
Filing a VICP claim is an easier process than winning a lawsuit, which takes time and effort and also demands a higher burden of proof.
“That’s why the whole vaccine injury system was set up,” Hotez said. “It was actually to the plaintiff’s benefit to get a faster judgment without having to show detailed evidence of proof.”

Without VICP, patients would need to pay lawyers a large chunk of their settlements, if their case moves through the courts at all, Reiss said: “The lack of contingency fee means they don’t have to pay 30% to 50% of their earnings through the lawyer.”

Compensating doctors for reporting side effects to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) risks offering “the wrong incentives” to unscrupulous providers who could increase such activities to become a new revenue source, Reiss said.

The changes could “certainly” be used by organizations such as Children’s Health Defense to legitimize its work spreading misinformation “and convince donors and others that they should give them more money”, she added.

VAERS, alongside several other vaccine monitoring systems, works well to pick up signals of very rare side effects, such as myocarditis from initial mRNA Covid vaccines and thrombotic thrombocytopenia in the Johnson and Johnson Covid vaccine, Hotez noted. But it’s not built to prove links between vaccines and certain side effects, as vaccination opponents have attempted to do, he said.

“The VAERS system was never meant to show cause and effect,” Hotez said. “It’s like looking for signs of alien communication in outer space. You look at every little blip, and almost all of them have nothing, are not real. But you have to analyze them.”

Years ago, Hotez engaged Kennedy in a series of conversations about misinformation that autism spectrum disorder is related to vaccines. Hotez pointed to known environmental influences on autism, like the anti-seizure medication valproic acid. Kennedy “had no interest then; he has no interest now”, Hotez said. “Even back then, there was a heavy emphasis on being a plaintiff attorney and suing vaccine companies. So that’s his narrow interest, which has nothing to do with reality – and he’s still going by the same playbook.”

Kennedy has attacked medical journals and schools, and funding for medical research has fallen sharply under his leadership. Such actions appear intended to “completely wipe out American medicine as we know it in favor of this whole system of grifting and pseudoscience”, Hotez said.

articles.title: Black voters helped Democrats win in Georgia. Now they expect to be heard
articles.summary:
Activists have been shouting about economic issues for years – in January they will expect lawmakers to respond

Stonecrest is resolutely middle class. About six out of 10 of its voters cast…

blocks.text: Stonecrest is resolutely middle class. About six out of 10 of its voters cast ballots in the 2026 election and about 90% of them voted for Democrats, according to election figures. And they have often been overlooked by Georgia’s Republican establishment.

The fundraiser Keisha Lance Bottoms held at the Privi event center and retreat in suburban Atlanta in September didn’t draw a lot of attention. But Stonecrest, by one measure the largest city in the United States with a non-Hispanic Black population above 90%, tends to roll under the radar.
It’s infuriating, said Vaughn Irons, Privi’s founder. “I think she came to speak to a community that often gets driven through and flown over.”
Black voting power helped secure victory for US Senator Jon Ossoff, Bottoms’ run for the governor’s race and a slew of down-ballot candidates. Now, those voters expect to be heard.

Culture war issues come with the change in partisan control of Georgia’s government; on abortion, on guns and on LGBTQ+ rights. But the customary politics of Georgia start and end with business, and that attitude is bipartisan.

Georgia’s Black voters have long wrestled with the Black Mecca paradox. Atlanta has long attracted Black professional talent from across the country and the world who were looking for strong African American political and cultural institutions and an economic environment perceived to give Black people an even shake.

But upward mobility for native-born Black Atlantans has been anemic. Black unemployment rates are lower in Atlanta than the nation overall. Georgia leads the nation for Black executive representation and recent income growth. But Georgia offers the worst chances for wealth of any state for a Black child born into poverty.
Activists have stood on soapboxes to shout at Georgia’s lawmakers about these economic issues for the last 20 years. In January, those voters will expect their government to answer them.

blocks.caption: ‘Vote Today Black Voters Matter’ and ‘It’s About Us’ signage on the lawn of a church in Atlanta, Georgia, on 3 November 2026.  Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: The opinions of Black voters – particularly Black women – have been ignored for years, said Tiffani Stephens, a voter in DeKalb county. “We’ve taken as the pretty person and all we care about is clothes, shoes and makeup,” she said. “Where if you really know a Black woman, you know these are additives. We are of substance. Deep substance.”

Democrats didn’t just win the marquee political contests in Georgia this November. They won every statewide election from the lieutenant governor’s office down to the insurance commissioner. Democrats displaced a Republican majority on the electricity rate-setting public service commission. Almost all the statewide office holders will be Black women, including the incoming speaker of the Georgia house, state representative Carolyn Hugley of Columbus. Democrats are one state senator short of controlling both chambers.

“This was not just a magical thing. This took a long time, building the infrastructure for the south and particularly for Georgia,” said Deborah Scott, executive director of Georgia STAND-UP, a “think and act tank” non-profit advocating for job training and economic development for working families.

It has taken multiple failed election cycles, chipping away at layers of cynicism, to be ready for this moment, Scott said. Stacey Abrams, two-time gubernatorial candidate turned democracy activist, deserves some credit for Georgia’s political results in November. But it is also the product of meticulous relationship-building groundwork, particularly by organizations led by Black women, she added.

“If Stacey is the tree that all of these newly elected officials are sitting in, then the roots of that are community-based organizations and non-profit organizations like Georgia STAND-UP and the People’s Agenda, folks that have been doing the work for a long time.”

blocks.caption: Stacey Abrams at the governor election night watch party, in Atlanta, on 9 November 2022. Photograph: Justin Kase/REX/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Describing the election results as a referendum on gas prices, or the war, or Donald Trump, is reductive, Scott said. Black voters assess their conditions holistically. “It’s not just about the gas prices are too damn high – which is true – but it’s also about the quality of life for regular Americans.”

The last two years have been radicalizing for some Georgia voters, Scott said. While highly-educated CDC employees found themselves impaled on the spear tips of HHS secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, nonprofits serving low-income communities like Scott’s have been scrambling to replace federal spending and a dearth of private grants, she said.
Before the election, activists have been squabbling for scarce resources, she said. Today, they are bathing in the afterglow of political unity.

For 20 years, Democrats have been shut out of major decisions about Georgia’s policy direction. The state has restrictive abortion laws and libertine gun laws. It is one of 10 states which did not expand access to Medicaid.

It has also attracted stunning amounts of foreign investment during Kemp’s two-terms in office, with car manufacturers, battery plants and chip makers locating to Georgia. But almost all of that state-directed economic development landed either in the north Georgia foothills or in rural south Georgia, like the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America manufacturing hub in Bryan county, rewarding white, Republican voters with jobs and political attention.

Scott speaks about the urgent need to encode voting rights protections in the Georgia constitution with one breath. In the next, she talks about deepening the port of Savannah, or the new Audi car plant being built near Macon.

“If you look at rural Georgia versus urban and suburban Georgia, it really is a tale of two states,” she said. “This is an opportunity for economic development in all of the regions around Georgia … it’s an opportunity to equalize the state. It’s Atlanta and the rest of the state. And of course, even in Atlanta, it’s the tale of two cities. Those that are born poor will not come out of it. There’s an opportunity for really affordable housing and real economic development.”

The city of Stonecrest, a suburb of south-eastern Atlanta, exists as a municipality because its Black, middle-class voters decided 10 years ago that they wanted their community to incorporate to serve them the way white middle-class voters are served 30 miles north in Sandy Springs. They wanted political leadership that matched their aspirations.

blocks.caption: A person shows the ‘I Voted’ sticker after voting in the midterm election in Atlanta, Georgia, USA, 03 November 2026.  Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPA

blocks.text: “As a small business owner, which I am, this is an opportunity to have a seat at the table,” said Kazemde Ajamu, who owns Akoma Coffee & Books at Stonecrest.

Ajamu is looking for Georgia to recognize microbusinesses and to better empower entrepreneurship for small business owners. “I feel good about the incoming governor-elect, that this gives us an opportunity to have a voice to speak to it, to create laws that help micro-businesses, mom-and-pops … That’s one example of having a seat at the table, having a voice, and someone that’s listening and can be proactive in that area.”

While Democrats have control over the apparatus of state government, there is no reason to believe that’s a permanent condition. Political competition will force Bottoms and the state legislature to pay attention everywhere, Irons said.

“Everybody’s interest is in growing, and having prosperity and better education,” Irons said. “The success of what’s likely to happen for the next governor is to create an environment where all parties that are serious about the growth and the prosperity of the state of Georgia can have a seat at the table.”

The accession of Bottoms as governor and Democrats in control of government agencies may mean that a place like Stonecrest is less likely to be overlooked, Irons said. But the former HUD official and economic development director for DeKalb county said that doesn’t alone solve problems.

“I think every community has to be ready for the investment that it wants,” Irons said. “And so you have a governor that you can access differently. I think Governor [Brian] Kemp probably was aware of the needs, but a different group of people had access, right? I think now that just because you have access doesn’t mean you don’t have your own responsibility to be ready.”

articles.title: Protest in Prague over media freedom expected to be one of biggest in Czechia’s history
articles.summary:
Hundreds of thousands expected to rally against plan to scrap licence fees and fund broadcasters from state budget

Hundreds of thousands of Czechs are expected to rally in Prague on Sunday…

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of Czechs are expected to rally in Prague on Sunday to protest against what they say is a government attempt to stifle media freedom.
The gathering to save the mandatory licence fees that fund Czechia’s public broadcasters could be one of the biggest in the nation’s history, organisers say.

It will mark the latest challenge to the prime minister, Andrej Babiš, and his coalition of populist, hard-right nationalist and Eurosceptic parties, and follows weeks of demonstrations in towns and cities and a strike by staff at Czech TV and Czech Radio.

Protesters say the plan to scrap licence fees and fund the broadcasters from the state budget would give ministers more leverage over newsrooms and follow the example of Slovakia, Hungary, Poland and Serbia, where current and previous rightwing populist governments eroded media independence.

The Million Moments for Democracy group that is organising the demonstration said the authorities would see the level of opposition. “Babiš and his government obviously think they will get away with anything … that they can ignore experts, silence critics and treat democratic institutions like their property,” it said in a statement.

The group expects 400,000 to 600,000 people at Letná Plain, which overlooks Prague’s historic centre. Some protesters would be channelling wider opposition to the government, said Daniel Stach, a TV presenter and one of the most recognised faces of the campaign.
The proposed changes, which would cut state television and radio budgets by about 15%, have drawn fire from international media organisations.

The European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have also criticised the government’s media plan and compared it to controversial moves by Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, and Hungary’s former premier, Viktor Orbán.

Babiš, a billionaire who returned to power last year, said protesters were riling up the public with unfounded claims about threats to media freedom. Last week he published an op-ed on what he called the “seven lies” being peddled by the opposition over the licence fees, which together add up to 205 koruna (£7.03) a month.

“Anyone who talks about ‘nationalisation’ [of public media] is deliberately lying,” he wrote, describing the criticism as “hysterical outbursts”. “Under no circumstances will we interfere in editorial work.”

articles.title: Three men sentenced to death in Jordan over fatal church mass shooting
articles.summary: The attack on funeral at a Greek Orthodox church killed nine and injured 34 others last month.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Nine people were killed in the shooting at the Greek Orthodox church last month
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for carrying out a fatal mass shooting on a church last month.
The attack on 23 October killed nine people and injured 34 others who had been attending a Christian funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.

Jordan's Armed Forces said in a statement on Sunday that the men had been convicted of committing "terrorist acts", as well as possessing weapons, "promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation" and "conspiracy to commit terrorist acts".
The three men - two Jordanian brothers and their brother-in-law - fled the scene of the attack and were arrested three days later. They have not been publicly identified.
Karak is home to a sizeable Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom.
CCTV footage from the day of the attack showed three men holding guns approaching and firing on St George's church in the village of Hmoud.
Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen near church
A second video showed dead and wounded people lying on the ground amid chaotic scenes at the church.
It is still unclear why the attackers chose to target that specific church.
Shortly after the attack, Jordan's King Abdullah II wrote on X: "The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation.
"Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity."
The three men fled the scene of the shooting and were later located inside an abandoned house in Karak governorate, south of the capital, Amman.

They refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and wounded all three of them, the Public Security Directorate said at the time. No security personnel were hurt in the shootout.

blocks.caption:
Map of Jordan showing the location of Hmoud in the west-central part of the country, south-west of Amman and near the Dead Sea. 

Neighbouring countries Israel and Saudi Arabia are labelled, with a locator globe showing Jordan’s position in the Middle East.

blocks.text: King Abdullah praised security forces for chasing the suspects "to the very end".
The week after the Karak shooting, Jordan struck what its military said were "terrorist organisations" in Syria in retaliation to the church attack.

Syrian health officials told state media that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike on a village in the southern Daraa province. Jordan said its fighter jets had killed and wounded "several terrorists" without giving further details.
Jordan said it had co-ordinated with the Syrian government, but Syria said it had not been notified in advance.
Executions in Jordan are carried out by hanging. The kingdom previously observed an unofficial ban on executions from 2006 to 2014, and another pause from 2017 until June this year.

articles.title: VP Sara impeachment: Defense seeks subpoenas for 4 witnesses on Cale88 issue
articles.summary: The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte has requested subpoenas to four individuals to appear as its next witnesses when the trial resumes on Nov. 19 and 20, Rep. Joel Chua said.

blocks.text: Published November 15, 2026 6:58pm Updated November 15, 2026 7:10pm

The defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte has requested that the impeachment court issue subpoenas to four individuals to appear as its next witnesses when the trial resumes on November 19 and 20, House prosecution panel member Joel Chua said.
The Manila lawmaker did not provide further details.
In its request for subpoenas, the defense identified the prospective witnesses as:

items: Atty. Rainer Dela Fuente of AML Consulting PH, who "will testify on fundamental legal concepts relating to the Anti-Money Laundering Act";

Dr. Ceferino S. Rodolfo, the Department of Trade and Industry's Undersecretary for Industry Development and Investment Promotions Group, who "will testify on matters relating to Cale88 Foods Corporation's registration with the Board of Investments";

Pilar Marilyn M. Pagayunan, MBA, Director IV of the Center for Food Regulation and Research of the Food and Drug Administration, who "will testify on matters relating to Cale88 Foods Corporation's product registration for its sweetened banana chips;"; and

Rowena G. Mendoza, General Manager III and/or any representative from the Center for International Expositions and Missions (CITEM), who "will testify on matters relating to Cale88 Foods Corporation communications, such as, but not limited to, electronic mail correspondences sent by CITEM to Cale88 and other invitations to the corporation for food expositions."

blocks.text: The defense panel earlier informed the impeachment court that it has eight to 10 witnesses remaining for the trial.
It remains unclear whether the defense panel will add more witnesses in the coming days.
Under the rules of the impeachment court, the defense and prosecution panels are directed to submit witnesses at least five days before the trial if those names are not in the pre-trial order.
Duterte has been impeached for alleged unexplained wealth. Three other articles of impeachment against her have been dropped by the prosecution. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Palace to protesters: Follow law in staging rallies
articles.summary: Malacañang on Sunday called on protesters to follow the law when staging demonstrations, as it defended authorities carrying out their mandate to maintain peace and order.

blocks.text: Published November 15, 2026 6:48pm
Malacañang on Sunday called on protesters to follow the law when staging demonstrations, as it defended authorities carrying out their mandate to maintain peace and order.

“Pag sinabing no rally zone, sana naman ay sumunod kayo sa polisiya kung ano ang itinatakda ng batas at kung ano ang sinasabi ng rules. Hindi pwedeng sabihin makabayan kayo kung sarili nating rules ay hindi nyo kayang tuparin,” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said during a press briefing.
(When an area is designated as a no-rally zone, I hope you follow the policies set by law and the rules. You cannot claim to be patriotic if you cannot follow our own rules.)
“Ang kapulisan, ang mandato nila ay magbigay ng peace and order. So hindi dahil meron kayong karapatan, ang kapulisan ay hindi kikilos para lamang pabayaan kayo na gumawa ng mga krimen,” she added.
(The police's mandate is to maintain peace and order. Having the right to protest does not mean the police cannot act and should simply allow you to commit crimes.)

According to GMA News' Darlene Cay, Manila Police District chief legal officer Police Capt. Felino Nabato said five individuals were arrested for causing a disturbance and holding a protest outside the designated freedom park.
Anakbayan, meanwhile, criticized authorities over what it described as the fouling of Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila, after human waste was reportedly seen at the freedom park on Sunday.
The group said the waste was found at the site where protesters planned to camp before staging a demonstration against the Pax Silica Initiative.
US President Donald Trump is scheduled to arrive in the Philippines on November 17 for the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.
His planned visit has drawn concerns from several civil society groups, many of which have announced protests to denounce his presence in the country.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Iran targets Bahrain airbase as strikes resume in Gulf - Middle East crisis live
articles.summary:
Bahrain lies directly across Persian Gulf from Iran and is home to US Navy Fifth Fleet

After two months of calm, the explosions have started again for Bahrain citizens.

Locals reported…

blocks.text: Opening summary

blocks.caption: Frances Mao

blocks.text: Frances Mao
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the fighting in the Middle East.
Iran has targeted an airbase in Bahrain in the latest resumption of strikes since September, prompting public warnings and sirens to ring out in the Gulf kingdom this morning.
According to Iranian media, the IRGC said it had sent six drones to attack a US radar system hosted in the US-allied island state.
Explosions were heard around the capital, Manama, but Bahrain authorities say their air defences intercepted the attacks before they reached their targets.

Bahrain, which lies directly across the Persian Gulf from Iran, is home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, and has been repeatedly attacked by Tehran during the course of the war, which has seen flare-ups in strikes amid long bouts of inaction.

There are fears Iran’s attacks this morning might signal a resumption of the war while US President Donald Trump has threatened but refrained from returning to major combat. Negotiations to end the war remain at a stalemate, with the US maintaining its naval blockade and Iran its stranglehold over the strait of Hormuz.
Developments in the Red Sea this morning will add to further concerns for Gulf oil flows.

The Yemeni government forces supported by Saudi Arabia, fighting the Houthis, have retreated from the Bab el-Mandeb area, giving the Iran-aligned rebels even greater control over the critical shipping lane, which Saudi Arabia and other Gulf oil producers had been relying on to get their supplies out.
Elsewhere, Hamas has confirmed that a senior commander involved in planning the 7 October attacks was killed in an Israeli airstrike on Saturday.
Stay with us for the latest.
Key events

items: 11m agoBahrain locals: 'I was hoping this period was behind us'
27m agoOpening summary
27m agoSecond attack in three days

blocks.text: Here’s a recap of what the various sides have said this morning regarding the latest Iranian strikes targeting a US air base in Bahrain.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards:

double quotation markThe US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force. The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response.
Bahrain’s foreign ministry
double quotation mark[Bahrain] rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks.
I’m yet to see a response from the US, but can expect Centcomm (which oversees all US military operations in the Middle East) to comment at some stage, like it did for Friday’s attack.
Bahrain locals: 'I was hoping this period was behind us'
After two months of calm, the explosions have started again for Bahrain citizens.
Locals reported hearing blasts about 4am local time, and then a second round at 6.30am.
double quotation markIt’s exactly what I was hoping wouldn’t happen: Iranian attacks starting again, with all the worry and uncertainty that go with them”, Hayat Ibrahim, 65, told AFP news agency.
Another resident, Mohammed Abdallah, a shopkeeper in the capital Manama, which is just north of the air base targeted said:
double quotation markI was hoping this period was behind us and wouldn’t happen again.
Bahrain’s Interior Ministry posted public warnings on X, telling “residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels”.
Iran had last launched strikes in the first week of September, when the regime targeted US military assets in Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait.

blocks.caption: Smoke seen in the sky in northern Bahrain following Iranian drone and missile attacks in early September. Photograph: UGC/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Second attack in three days
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they had launched six drones targeting a US air defence radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base on Sunday morning, reported Iranian media.
They said they had attacked the air base in retaliation for “hostile US actions”. The base is about a 30-minute drive south of Manama.

US forces have been quietly carrying out a series of strikes on Iranian sites in recent weeks, including on the key Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, where there’s a major IRGC presence. Trump has called them minor strikes.
Bahrain officials this morning have accused Tehran of continuing a “systematic hostile approach” to the kingdom.
The drone flurry this morning comes just 48 hours after Iran launched drones on Friday, the first escalations targeting Bahrain in two months.
That attack targeted an American radar facility. US Central Command said it had shot down the two drones without any injury or damage.

Bahrain officials hadn’t issued any warnings for that attack, but were forced to send out public alerts this morning telling residents to seek shelter. The Interior Ministry told locals to remain calm but proceed to to the nearest safe location.

articles.title: ASEAN adopts declaration on fair, ethical recruitment of migrant workers
articles.summary: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Sunday adopted a declaration promoting the fair, ethical and sustainable recruitment of migrant workers across the region.

blocks.text: Published November 15, 2026 6:03pm
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Sunday adopted a declaration promoting the fair, ethical and sustainable recruitment of migrant workers across the region.
Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac said the declaration would benefit about 600,000 migrant workers across ASEAN member states.

"With this declaration, magkakaroon ng greater transparency and accountability, mas malinaw, mas tapat at mas may pananagutan ang mga stakeholders, lalo sa larangan ng recruitment and placement ng migrant workers across ASEAN member states," Cacdac said during a press briefing.

(With this declaration, there will be greater transparency and accountability, with stakeholders becoming clearer, more honest and more accountable, particularly in the recruitment and placement of migrant workers across ASEAN member states.)
He said the declaration prohibits excessive or unreasonable recruitment fees and strengthens policies and regulations governing recruitment and manning agencies.

Cacdac added that ASEAN member states would coordinate to ensure safe and ethical recruitment practices, as well as cooperation in the rescue and repatriation of migrant workers and the possible apprehension of those involved in recruitment-related violations.
DMW Assistant Secretary Levinson Alcantara said the agency was preparing the necessary paperwork following the adoption of the declaration.
"Mayroon po kaming inaayos na paperwork. Sana pagkatapos nitong adoption by the end of November mayroon na tayong capacity training seminar," Alcantara said.
The initial implementation of the declaration could begin in early 2027, he added.
"So the soonest that we can have as an initial implementation of the declaration, following the declaration would probably be early 2027," Alcantara said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] A fellowship for the planet
articles.summary: 'I am going to Batangas to stay at a marine station with scientists working to bring citizen science closer to the public'

blocks.text: 'I am going to Batangas to stay at a marine station with scientists working to bring citizen science closer to the public'
Hello! I cover environmental issues for Rappler, and this year my focus for the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) lies on the ocean.
With Australia as co-president of the summit, Pacific priorities are high on the agenda. The summit is billed as the “Blue COP,” with an Antalya ocean declaration in the works.
The ocean is the world’s largest carbon sink. Being front and center of the climate negotiations has been a long time coming.

I am joining seven other journalists from around the world to cover COP31 remotely through the ocean lens. Among the big questions we hope to shed light on: How will countries integrate ocean solutions in the complex architecture of the global climate regime? This question brings with it a host of other issues such as funding sources.

On a personal level, the fellowship’s focus on oceans provides relief, giving me a single angle to latch on. Climate negotiations have their own language. Coverage of COPs requires dealing with a broad array of issues, such as poverty, displacement, hunger, waste, capitalism, wars, and even genocide. It requires a perspective that thinks in the big picture.

An example is the sobering reminder from Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during the leaders’ summit: “Today, one cannot speak of the future of the planet without speaking of the wars that target soil, water, air, natural resources, and human lives.”

The summit, despite its own language, does not happen in a silo. In the backdrop of COP31 is the global fuel crisis and the war in Iran, the ecocide in Gaza, the El Niño that threatens fishers and farmers — and, in our own backyard, the hectic preparations for the ASEAN Summit.

In every coverage we have always thought of ways to bring the COP to our readers. To deal with the local stories. This year, we are giving regular updates through our Muni chat app, making space for environmental advocates in our social and newsletter spaces. We mean to make conversations because this is where understanding starts (a fellowship of sorts).
We are also recording (probably as you read this) another The Green Report podcast episode to wrap the developments of the week. Something to listen to on your commute home.
In early November, as part of my fellowship, I visited a group of volunteer divers in Batangas who monitor coral bleaching in a marine reserve.

Next week, I am going back to Batangas, in a different town, to stay at a marine station with scientists working to bring citizen science closer to the public. Their dream? That the ordinary fisherman learns to watch the waters, the changes in colors of the coral reef.

The COP is much about these communities on the ground as it is about the negotiators who deal in high-level, closed door meetings. We aim to report the stories from this broad spectrum to light. For starters, you can join our Muni chat here, or follow the COP stories from this page. – Rappler.com

articles.title: It started with a lobster dinner. Now it's an East Coast institution
articles.summary: The Shore Club in Hubbards, N.S., has spent more than eight decades serving up classic lobster suppers and live music to people from around the globe. A new CBC documentary pulls back the curtain on…

image.caption: The lobster suppers at the Shore Club started in 1936 in the tiny community of Hubbards, N.S., while the dance hall was built 10 years later. Today, it's a worldwide word-of-mouth phenomenon. (CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia

The Shore Club in Hubbards, N.S., has spent more than eight decades serving up classic lobster suppers and live music to people from around the globe. A new CBC documentary pulls back the curtain on how the Harnish family managed to turn a rural dance hall into a Maritime institution.
CBC documentary explores impact, evolution of The Shore Club in Hubbards, N.S.

Standing shoulder-to-shoulder on the edge of a picturesque Nova Scotia cove, thousands of roaring fans watched the sun melt into a sky brushed with amber and blue, eagerly awaiting rocker Matt Mays to strike his first chord.

The outdoor festival took place just outside The Shore Club, a historic music venue and lobster supper hall in the tiny community of Hubbards that has endured for 90 years and draws visitors from across the globe.
After playing inside the wooden building every summer for decades, Mays admitted he initially worried whether its signature “magic” would follow him outdoors. It did.
“It's one of those places on earth that all the vibes are,” Mays said in a new CBC documentary about the club.
“It's a very spiritual event for myself … and if it's spiritual, that means it's just bigger than anything.”

The outdoor shows at the Shore Club represent yet another evolution in the story of how a quaint venue in a rural South Shore hamlet at the end of a winding road became a world famous Maritime institution.
For 80 years, East Coast musicians and fans have revered this venue
Each summer, the family-run business draws thousands to its classic lobster suppers, electric concerts, camping under lofty pines and basking on its private beach.
The venue has gained a reputation among big Canadian artists and music fans for its distinct atmosphere and long-standing traditions.
Its unique Maritime esthetic has drawn the likes of Kentucky Fried Chicken founder Colonel Sanders, Mariah Carey, and Prince Charles and Lady Diana.
But the club is always evolving, while staying true to its roots. It’s a balancing act the Harnish family, which operates the club, has done for nine decades.
Still, its allure isn’t something they can put their finger on.

“At any given night in this room, we'll have people from almost every continent on earth in here.... You realize this is a really unique and fun and amazing place to be,” said Luke Harnish, sitting in the club’s dining hall and dance floor next to his father, Rhys Harnish.
"Dad and I looked at each other dumbfounded many times this summer, just like, why does this work?"

articles.title: Police arrest anti-Pax Silica protesters as ASEAN Summit opens in Manila
articles.summary: At least 11 protesters were arrested by police within the freedom park, according to Manila Police District Spokesperson Philip Ines

blocks.text: PAX SILICA PROTEST. Militants gather at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila on November 15, 2026, to protest the proposed Pax Silica initiative and US President Donald Trump’s visit to the 49th ASEAN Summit.
Rappler
At least 11 protesters were arrested by police within the freedom park, according to Manila Police District Spokesperson Philip Ines

MANILA, Philippines – Police clashed with protesters at Liwasang Bonifacio on Sunday morning, November 15, as activists opposing Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump tried to march toward the ASEAN Summit venue.
The protesters were trying to reach the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC), the venue of the 49th ASEAN Summit.

Police blocked the protesters from proceeding to the summit venue. Some of the protesters managed to slip through several layers of policemen armed with shields. The cops, however, managed to block the protesters again.

blocks.caption: ASEAN PROTEST. Protesters scuffle with police officers in Manila on November 15, 2026, during a protest against US President Donald Trump’s upcoming visit and participation in the 49th ASEAN Summit.

blocks.text: Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) President Jerome Adonis said police told them they could not hold a street protest because they did not have a permit.

After nearly an hour of attempts to march to PICC, the protesters retreated to Liwasang Bonifacio. Despite this, at least 11 protesters were arrested by police within freedom park, according to Manila Police District Spokesperson Philip Ines.
Ines said at least 16 personnel from the Manila Police District were injured.
Cops dragged protesters into a police vehicle. Some officers were seen slapping, kicking, and punching one activist as they took him away.
Adonis questioned the legality of the arrests, saying they were made inside a freedom park.

blocks.caption: ASEAN PROTEST. Police arrest a protester in Liwasang Bonifacio on the opening of the ASEAN Summit in Manila, on Sunday, November 15. Photo by Patrick Cruz/Rappler

blocks.text: “Ang gulo ho nanggaling sa pulis. Hindi po galing sa amin. Nagdedepensa lang kami ng hanay namin,” he added. (The trouble started with the police, not us. We were only defending our ranks.)
Rappler asked the Manila Police District why the protesters were arrested, but it had yet to respond as of writing.
Under the Revised Penal Code, a person arrested without a warrant should be brought to court within a maximum of 36 hours, and that is for grave violations.
Police also towed the truck that protesters had used as a makeshift stage. Adonis accused police of puncturing their vehicles with nails.
In Liwasang Bonifacio, where the protesters plan to camp out, human manure was scattered in front of the statue of Andres Bonifacio, the “father of the Philippine revolution.”

blocks.caption: ASEAN PROTEST. Personnel from the Manila Department of Environment and Public Service clean the human manure scattered in front of the statue of Andres Bonifacio, in Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila, on Sunday, November 15. Photo by Patrick Cruz/Rappler

blocks.text: Bayan Muna Chairperson Teddy Casiño, who was also at the protest, claimed that the police were behind this.

“Isang malaking ka-hipokrituhan ang ginagawa ng gobyerno. Nagpapakita ng hospitality sa mga dayuhan pero binabastos ang kanyang mga mamamayan,” Casiño said. (The government’s actions are widely hypocritical. It shows hospitality to foreign visitors while disrespecting its own people.)
Personnel from the Manila Department of Environment and Public Service later cleaned the human manure.
Protesters have raised concerns that Pax Silica could displace Indigenous peoples and farming communities in the planned 4,000-acre industrial hub in New Clark City, Tarlac.

Pax Silica is a US-led initiative that seeks to strengthen supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors through partnerships with other countries. The signing of the Pax Silica agreement had reportedly been targeted for November, coinciding with Trump’s visit to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit.
Trump is expected to arrive in Manila on Tuesday, November 17, for the Special ASEAN-US Summit.
However, Department of Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo clarified that the Philippines would not sign the agreement during the 49th ASEAN Summit.
“We do not want to distract attention or take away attention from the regional initiatives that ASEAN and the Philippines are proposing,” Rodolfo told reporters on Tuesday, November 10.
Despite the delay, the Philippines eyes to sign the deal with the US before the year ends, Rodolfo said.
Amid the protests, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro appealed to the public to reconsider holding demonstrations during the summit.

“Whatever their demands may be, I hope these are not pursued through protests, although I recognize that this is their right. In these times, however, it would be better to have more in-depth discussions about whatever concerns the students may have,” Castro said during a press briefing on Saturday, November 14.
Prior to the Sunday protest, thousands of students also protested against Pax Silica. – Rappler.com

articles.title: A man was once murdered over the pronunciation of 'Newfoundland'
articles.summary: Newfoundlanders and Labradorians tend to feel strongly about the right way to pronounce the name of our island, but would you kill a man over it? In 1876, someone did.

image.caption: Two saw mill workers came to blows over the pronunciation of 'Newfoundland,' leading to a fatal shooting. (The Strand Magazine, 1898.)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
Newfoundlanders and Labradorians tend to feel strongly about the right way to pronounce the name of our island, but would you kill a man over it? In 1876, someone did.
Old West dispute over pronunciation led to lethal shooting, a midnight getaway, deathbed confession

Since the release of the Netflix limited series Below, the pronunciation of “Newfoundland” has become a hot topic once again. Actors are correcting talk show hosts; online commenters are correcting actors.
While these discussions can get pretty heated, they’re nothing compared to a fight that broke out over the word exactly 150 years ago.

One Friday night in March of 1876, workers from the Hooker and Gray saw mill near Larkspur, Colorado, were chatting over supper when their landlady asked one of them, a burly New Yorker named William Atcheson, about his dog.
It was a New-FOUND-land dog, Atcheson explained. No, it wasn’t, another man interjected. It was a New-found-LAND.
The objector was John Peter Davis, a Texan teamster in his mid-thirties who was rumoured to have been a gunslinger in his youth.

The murder occurred at a backwoods lumber mill on Colorado’s Great Divide, which might have looked similar to this mill in Williamstown, New York, photographed around 1900. (Oswego County Historical Society)

This wasn’t the first time the two men had clashed. Atcheson had more formal education than many of the other men on staff, and his zeal for “proper” word use had sometimes caused him to butt heads with the workers from Texas and with Davis, who acted as their spokesman.
Tensions had been rising, and this time they boiled over. “High words and some rather hard names” were exchanged, according to a report published in The Colorado Banner.

On their way to Atcheson’s shanty to consult a dictionary — and the mere fact that he had brought a dictionary to an isolated lumber camp on the frontier may tell you something of his passion for the English language — Atcheson took a swing at Davis and landed a blow so hard it knocked the Texan to the ground.
When Davis staggered to his feet, he had a revolver in his hand, and “true to his Texan breeding and education,” as one newspaper told it, he shot Atcheson in the gut.
Atcheson remained a tough customer until the end. As he lay bleeding, he bragged about having decked Davis twice more despite the bullet lodged in his belly.

Atcheson died in the early hours of Saturday morning, and Davis fled into the woods, leaving his team of draft animals behind. Witnesses said he was distraught he’d killed someone over such a trivial argument.
A simple question about a worker’s Newfoundland dog sparked the argument. (Edwin Landseer/Victoria and Albert Museum)
A snowstorm obliterated Davis’ tracks, and, though the local sheriff led a posse in after him, he was never found.
Had the two men made it as far as the dictionary, they would have discovered it disagreed with them both.
The 1864 edition of Webster, which would have been the latest version, gave the pronunciation as NEW-fund-LAND, with primary stress on the first syllable and secondary stress on the third.
Webster’s advice is strikingly similar to the way many Newfoundlanders and Labradorians say the word today, but how did Newfoundlanders pronounce the island’s name in the 1800s?

Until the early 20th century, the official pronunciation was NEW-FOUND-LAND, where each syllable was fully articulated and equally stressed. This was the pronunciation recommended by the Broadcasting Corporation of Newfoundland in 1939, though they allowed for “a slight stressing of the final syllable.”
The Rocky Mountain News called Atcheson and Davis “chronic disputants” who “always manifested much temper in their discussions." (Colorado Historic Newspapers Collection)
It was Joey Smallwood and the Newfoundland Historical Society who, in the late 1930s, advocated for the pronunciation New-fund-LAND.

Assuming neither Atcheson nor Davis was reducing “land” to “lund,” which has always been the cardinal sin of pronunciation among Newfoundlanders, the versions both men used could probably have been heard somewhere on the island in the 19th century.
Not that either Atcheson or Davis would have known that. There’s no evidence either man had any ties to Newfoundland itself.
The story might have ended there except for a letter that arrived on the doorstep of the Castle Rock, Colo., sheriff in late 1912.
The message purported to be written by a physician in Peoria, Ore., who was treating John Peter Davis, now 70 years old.

Believing himself to be at the brink of death, Davis had apparently confessed to Atcheson’s murder. Then, either he had asked the doctor to send his statement to the Colorado authorities to unburden his soul, or the doctor had taken it upon himself to turn Davis in so he could line his pockets with any reward money that might be on offer.
Whatever the case, the letter’s description of the crime was so specific the sheriff had no doubt it was sent by someone close to the killer.
When the story of the deathbed confession leaked to the media, reporters wondered “whether justice [would] be defeated by death,” but justice was also threatened by practical details.
Calls to Peoria failed to turn up any resident by the name of John Davis. If he was indeed living there, he had probably assumed a new identity.
Thirty-six years after the crime, the sheriff of Castle Rock received a letter from a man in Peoria, Ore., confessing to the killing. (The Herald Democrat/Colorado Historic Newspapers Collection)
Meanwhile, even if Davis survived his illness, were located, and were arrested, there might not be enough evidence left to convict him.

Older Coloradans remembered the unusual killing, but no official records of it could be found among county court documents or coroner’s reports. The physician who had treated Atcheson in his final hours was dead, and the prime witness was missing.
If Davis retracted his confession, there could be no trial. It’s not clear whether he was ever brought up on charges.
The case has a final irony.

William Atcheson was a man so devoted to proper word use he died over it, but none of the news reports of his death can agree on the spelling of his name, which is recorded as Atcheson, Atchison, Atchinson and Atherson.

articles.title: Fifth Canadian soldier dies from injuries caused by large fire at military base
articles.summary: Pte William Douglas Dal Bianco died from his injuries on Friday, a month after a fire that tore through CFB Wainwright.

blocks.text: Members of 1 Canadian Mechanized Brigade Group had been conducting live-fire training at the base, in the province of Alberta, when the fire broke out.
Military officials said at the time that the fire spread across a kilometre in a matter of seconds, taking many of those on the base by surprise.
Firefighters battled the blaze through the night, while nearby hospitals became inundated by injured personnel and staff.
Carney described it as "one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime".
An investigation found that the fire was likely sparked by a grenade launcher being fired on the base's grenade range, officials said.
Firefighters on the base had known about the fire but could not tackle it because it was in a danger area that could contain unspent explosives.

Canadian Chief of the Defence Staff Gen Jennie Carignan said the nation's armed forces were "heartbroken" by the loss of Dal Bianco, while Defence Minister David McGuinty offered his "deepest condolences" to his family, friends and colleagues.
"No words can ease the pain of losing a loved one, and my thoughts remain with all those affected by this tragedy," he said.

"We remain committed to supporting the families and the Canadian Armed Forces community during this profoundly difficult time, and to honouring Private Dal Bianco's service, dedication and sacrifice to Canada."

articles.title: Brazilian President Lula invites Marcos to visit Brazil
articles.summary: Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva invited President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to visit Brazil next year, as the two countries recently held bilateral talks in Manila.

blocks.text: Published November 15, 2026 5:12pm
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva invited President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to visit Brazil next year, as the two countries recently held bilateral talks in Manila.
Da Silva made the statement during a press briefing on Sunday as he concludes his two-day visit to the Philippines, according to GMA News Bea Pinlac's social media post.
He said Marcos was among the heads of state he invited to visit Brazil.
“We’re inviting everyone to come and visit Brazil,” Da Silva said, which was translated in English by a device provided by the Brazil delegation.
He added that Brazil aims to promote and collaborate with other countries in “exploration, transformation, industrialization,” among others.
Da Silva also hopes that Brazil will be a "definitive partner of ASEAN."
Malacañang said it has yet to confirm Brazil's invitation through the Department of Foreign Affairs.
Da Silva's visit coincided with the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits being held from November 15 to 17 in Pasay City.
Brazil, meanwhile, is a sectoral dialogue partner of ASEAN.
The bilateral meeting between the Philippines and Brazil tackled ways to enhance relations between the two countries.
The talks of the two leaders covered cooperation in multilateral forums and among countries of the Global South, according to the Presidential Communications Office.
Lula’s state visit also marks the first time a sitting Brazilian president visited the Philippines.
It also coincides with the 80th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries this year.—Mariel Celine Serquiña/RF, GMA News

articles.title: Canada is spending more than ever on health care. Are we getting our money's worth?

image.caption: Long wait times, difficulty finding family doctors and gaps in services have prompted health policy experts to question whether Canada's health-care system needs more fundamental changes to how care is delivered. (CBC News )

blocks.text: Canada is spending more on health care than ever. Whether Canadians are getting more care for their money is another question.

A new report from the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI), an independent, non-profit organization that collects and analyzes data on Canada's health-care system, projects health-care spending will reach a record $433 billion in 2026, or $10,398 per person, an increase of 4.8 per cent over last year.
For the first time since the pandemic, inflation-adjusted spending per person is expected to surpass its previous peak, reached in 2021.

But Canada already ranks among the higher-spending countries in the developed world, while patients continue to struggle with long wait times, overcrowded hospitals and difficulty finding family doctors.
That raises a central question: Is Canada spending enough on health care, or does the problem lie in how that money is being spent?

"I believe that these records of spending are just buying us more of the same right now," said Jason Sutherland, a professor at the University of British Columbia in Vancouver and director of the Centre for Health Services and Policy Research.
He argues that without substantial changes to how health care is organized and delivered, additional spending is unlikely to produce meaningful improvements for patients.
1 in 10 Canadians waiting more than 14 hours in emergency rooms: report
Is $10,000 per person a lot?

The $10,398 figure represents the combined cost of publicly and privately funded health care, including hospitals, doctors, prescription drugs and services paid for through private insurance or directly by patients. It is not the amount each Canadian pays in taxes.
While the figure may seem substantial, international comparisons provide important context.
According to the CIHI report, Canada devoted 11.5 per cent of its gross domestic product to health care in 2024, compared with an OECD average of 9.3 per cent.
That placed Canada alongside other high-spending countries, including France at 11.3 per cent and Sweden at 11.2 per cent, but below Germany at 12.2 per cent and the United States at 17.2 per cent.
"We are not cheap in our health-care spending," Sutherland said.
LISTEN | Ontario doctors demand an apology over provincial letters urging reduced hours and delayed care:
Here and Now Toronto7:49Why is the Ontario Ministry of Health asking doctors to scale back their hours and delay patient care?

Sara Allin, an associate professor at the University of Toronto's Institute of Health Policy, Management and Evaluation, agreed that Canada's spending is substantial. But she said the more revealing comparison is what countries achieve with their investments.
She pointed to data showing Canada performs relatively well on some measures, including life expectancy and vaccination rates, but continues to lag in important areas of access and service delivery.
"We have very persistently long wait times," Allin said. "We have persistent challenges with care co-ordination."
She described Canada's health system as generally a middle performer among countries with similarly high expenditures.
His cancer drug costs $90,000/month. Doctors say it’s greed
More money, but where is it going?
The CIHI report identifies a potentially important change in how health-care spending is growing.
Inflation-adjusted spending per person is projected to grow 2.3 per cent this year, compared with just 0.4 per cent in 2025.
More significantly, CIHI estimates public-sector spending will increase by more than $5 billion beyond what is needed to keep pace with inflation and demographic changes.

Adam Rondeau, CIHI's manager of health spending and operations analytics, said the increase could be an early indication that governments are investing in additional capacity, new technologies and innovations in health-care delivery.
But determining precisely where that money is going is more complicated.

items: Your genes could change your prescription. So why aren't doctors testing?
Your questions about this year's federal budget, answered

blocks.text: "It's difficult to say X number of dollars is net new and related to a given program of work," Rondeau said.
He explained that the report identifies additional spending but cannot establish whether that investment is producing shorter wait times, more available services or better patient outcomes.
Meanwhile, the report states that spending on physicians is projected to increase 8.3 per cent this year, substantially faster than overall health-care spending.
Yet access to primary care remains a major challenge. CIHI's research on primary care found that 17 per cent of Canadian adults reported having no regular health-care provider in 2023.

Sara Allin, an associate professor of health policy at the University of Toronto, says Canada spends more on health care than many comparable countries, but it continues to struggle with long wait times and access to services. (Submitted by Sara Allin)
Spending more isn't necessarily spending better
For Allin, the challenge isn't simply increasing health-care budgets; it's ensuring that additional investment produces measurable improvements.
"If we're spending this much, it's more perhaps how we're spending it than the level of spending at this point in terms of driving further improvements," she said.
One important difference between Canada and some comparable countries, she said, is how health care is financed.
According to CIHI's expenditure figures, 71.4 per cent of Canada's health spending is projected to come from public sources in 2026, with the remaining 28.6 per cent financed privately.

Allin said several other wealthy countries fund a larger share of health care collectively, allowing them to cover a broader range of services, including prescription drugs, dental care and mental health supports.
She said those differences have consequences for both efficiency and equity.
Publicly financed systems can negotiate lower prices and reduce some administrative costs, she explained. They can also reduce financial barriers that prevent patients from accessing needed services.
Hundreds of unionized health-care workers rally outside legislature
Allin said gaps in Canada's public coverage mean people without adequate private insurance can face substantial costs for necessary services, particularly prescription drugs and mental health care.
She also questioned whether Canada's health-care financing arrangements provide sufficient incentives to improve patient outcomes.
Rather than simply paying providers according to the volume of services delivered, Allin said governments could do more to link funding with measurable improvements in care.
Sutherland similarly argued that governments need to rethink where additional resources are directed.

items: Canada's health ministers say federal funding extension only delays looming 'fiscal cliff'
Cost of Canadian Dental Care Plan exceeded budget by $1.1B in first 2 years: auditor general

blocks.text: He pointed to home care, assisted living, long-term care and other community-based services as areas where greater investment could help keep patients out of overcrowded hospitals and emergency departments.
Both experts also raised concerns about the pressure that rising health-care spending could place on other public priorities, including education, housing and social services.

Ultimately, Sutherland said, the figures should reassure Canadians that substantial resources are being devoted to health care while also prompting them to question whether those resources are being used effectively.

"I think they should be somewhat relieved that Canada is not underfunding this health-care system, but at the same time, they should be concerned that they're not getting great value for their money."
