He is said to have told the auction house the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis.
The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

articles.title: COP31: Protesters, UN urge swift climate deal
articles.summary: The UN climate chief warned that "tactical delays" at the COP31 climate talks in Turkey could prevent a deal to slow global warming.

image.caption: Protesters outside the COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, lament the lack of progress on climate change Image: Umit Bektas/REUTERS

blocks.text: The United Nations' top climate official urged negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey to "avoid tactical delays" that would prevent a deal to stop global warming.
Delegates from more than 200 nations are gathered in the Mediterranean city of Antalya with the core goal of preventing the planet from warming by 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit).
Downtown, thousands of civil society and environmental activists from around the world protested against the consequences of climate change.
COP31: Can electrification replace fossil fuels?
What did the UN climate chief say?
Simon Stiell, Executive Secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), said getting an agreement is "tough but vital work."
"There ​is no collective success without compromise from every party," he added.
"As we head into the second week, ​I urge ‌parties to move swiftly to the hardest issues and to avoid tactical delays."

blocks.caption: Unlike previous UN climate summits, expectations for COP31 are mutedImage: Murad Sezer/REUTERS

blocks.text: Climate crisis pushed down agenda

With inflation, wars, deindustrialization and debt being seen as bigger immediate threats, many governments are watering down their commitments to the clean energy transition, along with the billions required to help developing nations to adapt.
The United ⁠States has snubbed the talks ​for the second year in a row under President Donald Trump, who has called climate change a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.
Delegates also face pressure from large fossil-fuel-producing nations to avoid setting stricter targets for a faster phase-out of oil and gas.
Climate advocates in Antalya are growing increasingly frustrated by the lack of commitment and delaying tactics preventing an ambitious deal.
COP31 is seeking to unlock finance and investment, reduce the use of so-called super-pollutants and methane and ensure food security.

blocks.caption: The COP31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, runs until November 19Image: Ozan Kose/AFP

blocks.text: Turkey seeks electrification deal
Host Turkey is, meanwhile, pushing a plan to expand global electrification. Yet, some environmental groups are disappointed the proposal doesn't push increased electricity use from renewable sources.
A UN report last month warned that, within a few years, the world is set to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius warming threshold, set in Paris in 2015.
This is the figure most scientists believe should stop the worst effects of climate change.
A first draft of a deal text is expected to emerge next week, according to Australia's ​COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen.
Climate protest draws activists from around the world
Meanwhile, tens of thousands of protesters marched through Antalya on Saturday for climate protection and human rights, according to the organizers.
Many were dismayed at the lack of progress and how the climate crisis is taking a back seat.

"The pursuit of profit at all costs continues to set the [global] agenda [and] govern the trajectory of our world, so there is a need to push back," environmental activist Zaki Mamdoo from South Africa told DW.
Luisa Nebauer, the main organizer of Germany's Fridays for Future movement, lamented that Chancellor Friedrich Merz was absent from the conference, along with several other European leaders.
"We won't have a chance to solve any of the crises as long as our planet is destabilizing by the hour," Nebauer told DW. "We must show up!"
Turkish authorities permitted the rally to go ahead, in a country that often bans large public gatherings.
Alongside the march, a parallel "People's Climate Summit" involving hundreds of domestic and international civil society groups takes place in Antalya this weekend.
As Turkey hosts COP31 its beaches are becoming too hot for sea turtles

articles.title: Copper wire upgrade caused nationwide flight suspension, US transport secretary says
articles.summary: The US government is trying to find out whether the chaos was caused by "incompetence" or faulty equipment.

blocks.text: 'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop
ByGeorge Wright and Helen Davidson
A nationwide US ground stop that caused thousands of flight cancellations was caused by an issue following a copper wire upgrade, Transport Secretary Sean Duffy said.
Duffy told a news conference that the government was trying to find out whether the problem was caused by "incompetence" on the part of the company doing the upgrades, or faulty equipment.
The US government does not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack, although an investigation is still under way, Duffy said.
Friday's suspension was the longest such incident since the 11 September 2001 attacks on the US and the disruption is expected to last for days.
Maintenance was being carried out to switch from copper wire to fibre by a contractor called L3Harris, a technology provider company, Duffy said.
The US has "an incredibly old telecommunications system", he added.
"It was such an old wire that it was being discontinued," he said.

The transport secretary explained that a router that was being worked on had started flooding other air traffic control systems and created communication issues with planes which led the government to shut down the airspace for safety reasons.
Bryan Bedford, who heads the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), told the same news conference: "We see zero evidence of anything nefarious, and zero evidence of anything AI related."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Duffy told a news conference that the US government did not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Duffy told a news conference that the US government did not believe it was as a result of a cyber-attack
No flights were allowed to take off from the continental US for more than four hours from 15:54 EST (19:54 GMT) on Friday.
More than 3,500 flights were cancelled and more than 2,000 delayed in the US on Saturday, according to tracking website Flight Aware, as knock-on disruption continues.

In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to the gates. Some international flights were allowed to depart US airports, in an apparent effort to clear space.
Duffy warned that a similar issue could arise again unless the US Congress approved upgrades to air traffic control infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump has requested $30.1bn for the upgrades. Both chambers of Congress are currently controlled by the Republican Party.
Questions remain on why US ground stop happened when it did, former TSA boss says

Former TSA Administrator John Pistole told the BBC that "the fact that they were able to get it restarted in four-and-a-half hours is good news - it shows a resilience in the system - but what's to say it's not going to happen tomorrow?"
A nationwide ground stop has only been ordered one other time since all flights were banned from take-off for several days following the 11 September 2001 attacks.

articles.title: Italy fines Meta €805m over accessing users' photos
articles.summary: The social media giant is accused of not informing about 20 million users it had access to their photos.

blocks.text: Italian regulators have fined social media giant Meta €805m (£670; $887m) for accessing Android users' photos without their specific consent.
Italy's Data Protection Authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.
It has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately.
The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.
The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts.

Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in their gallery.

The regulator said it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".
It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation".
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment.
Last month, Meta, which is also behind Instagram and WhatsApp, was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.
A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) after it found that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

articles.title: Nigeria cautions against travel via Ethiopia's main airport due to altitude
articles.summary: The foreign ministry in Abuja says 6 Nigerians with underlying health problems have died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.

blocks.text: Nigeria's government has cautioned its citizens, in particular those with medical conditions, against travelling via Ethiopia's main airport due to its altitude.
The foreign ministry in Abuja said 16 Nigerians with underlying health problems had died this year while transiting through Addis Ababa.

The city sits at an altitude of 2,334m (7,657ft) above sea level, making it one of the highest capitals in the world. Bole International Airport is a major hub for travel between Africa, the Middle East and Asia, serving millions of passengers a year.
Nigeria said those with cardiovascular and respiratory conditions were at an increased risk.
The Nigerian foreign ministry did not disclose the identities of the travellers it said had died, nor the cause of death.
It urged anyone with a health condition exacerbated by high altitudes to "exercise caution" when planning a journey via Addis Ababa and "obtain appropriate medical guidance" before doing so.
The ministry stressed that it did not want to discourage Nigerians from travelling through the Ethiopian capital.
Visiting an area at a high altitude can be dangerous for people with heart and lung diseases, as the air is thinner and so less oxygen can get into the bloodstream, experts say.

This means the heart has to work harder to get enough oxygen to different parts of the body, which can sometimes lead to heart failure among those with existing conditions, according to the American Heart Association.

The lack of oxygen at high altitudes can cause adverse effects such as dizziness, fatigue and shortness of breath among healthy people - which can cause complications for people with lung disease, studies show.

articles.title: Werner Holzer Prize awarded to Katja Gloger and DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim
articles.summary: DW journalist Jaafar Abdul Karim and Russia correspondent Katja Gloger have been awarded the prestigious Werner Holzer Prize for international journalism.

image.caption: Jaafar Abdul Karim (left) and Katja Gloger were the proud winners of the award for outstanding international journalismImage: Sven Moschitz

blocks.text: At a time when press freedom is under pressure and international newsrooms are shrinking, the Werner Holzer Prize celebrates a profession that many consider indispensable to democracy: foreign correspondence.

Presented in honor of Werner Holzer, the veteran reporter and former editor-in-chief of the German daily newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau, this year's award coincided with what would have been his 100th birthday. Holzer spent decades reporting from some of the world's most important hot spots and championing international journalism.

At the award ceremony in Frankfurt's Römer, the city's historic town hall, Mayor Mike Josef recalled that fundamental rights such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press were first enshrined for all Germans by the Frankfurt Parliament in the nearby Paulskirche in 1848.
Germany's public broadcasters under fire from far-right AfD

The 2026 winners reflect the breadth and ambition of the award. First prize went to Katja Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent who moved to Moscow in 1989 and accompanied Vladimir Putin during the early years of his presidency.

In her recent nonfiction book, "The Failure: An Investigative Report of Germany's Russia Policy," Gloger and co-author Georg Mascolo offer a searing critique of the misjudgments and illusions that shaped German policy toward Russia for decades.

Second prize was awarded to DW journalist and presenter Jaafar Abdul Karim. His talk show JaafarTalk reaches millions of viewers across the Arab world and in Germany. Whether in Tunis, Beirut or Cairo, Abdul Karim tackles subjects that are often considered taboo.

A research grant went to freelance journalist Luise Land, whose current project explores why her German-Namibian family still owns extensive landholdings in Namibia today. By tracing that history, she examines the enduring legacy of the genocide against the Herero and Nama peoples by German colonial forces in the early 20th century.
Call for more international coverage

"Katja Gloger is one of the leading foreign policy reporters. For decades, she has been among the foremost experts on Russia and speaks out on uncomfortable truths," the jury stated on Friday, explaining its decision to honor Gloger. "Like almost no one else, she has gained access to the very heart of the Kremlin's power elite — from Mikhail Gorbachev to Vladimir Putin."

At the prize-giving ceremony, Gloger delivered a passionate plea for more journalism — and more international coverage — in the German press. "We must defend trustworthy, reliable and fact-based journalism with everything in our power," she said.
Why press freedom matters to everyone, not just journalists

Gloger worked for Reporters Without Borders for 12 years. "The latest rankings show that only one in 100 people can get their information from free, independent journalism and a free, independent press. That shows what's at stake," she said.

The prize winner also said she would dedicate the award to journalists in exile and to her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta, the independent Russian newspaper long known for its critical reporting on the Kremlin. Earlier this week, the paper was forced to shut down its operations in Russia and leave its Moscow newsroom.
Belief in the power of dialogue

In his acceptance speech, Jaafar Abdul Karim said journalism has become more challenging and exhausting than ever. The DW host spoke of hatred and incitement, attacks and threats, both online and offline, in the regions he reports on as well as in Germany.

Such pressure, he said, takes a personal toll — yet giving up is not an option. "When I listen to my heart, I know I have to keep going," he said. The answer, he argued, is a form of journalism that fosters dialogue, embraces multiple perspectives and helps bridge divides rather than deepen them.

"I firmly believe in the power of dialogue, today more than ever. That's why we must talk to one another. Even when it gets difficult. Even when we disagree. Or perhaps precisely because of that," he said.

blocks.caption: 'When everyone jumps to conclusions, we need journalists who ask questions first,' said DW's Jaafar Abdul KarimImage: Sven Moschitz

blocks.text: Listening doesn't mean agreeing, and understanding doesn't mean being in agreement. "Especially now, in times of polarization, when those who believe they're always right are often the loudest, we as journalists have a special responsibility. When everyone is just shouting into their own bubbles or communities, we need journalists who connect these bubbles with one another," he said.

The jury praised Abdul Karim for creating programs at DW that reach millions of young people across the Arab world and in Germany. "His journalism fosters dialogue between countries, between generations, and between religions. He has set new standards," the jury stated.

So far in 2026, JaafarTalk has already garnered more than 1.1 billion views across all platforms, and its community has grown to more than 9 million followers. Its motto: "Diversity fosters dialogue."

"We need fact-based journalism that promotes dialogue and reflects the diversity of our society," Abdul Karim stressed. "By that, I mean an honest and open dialogue in which we do not look away or remain silent. On the contrary, we must take a clear stand against racism, antisemitism, Islamophobia, discrimination, sexism, and hate speech — no matter which side they come from."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: How a US extradition bid over Hamas allegations put a wealthy activist before a Spanish court
articles.summary:
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, a Cox Enterprises heir, faced a two-hour hearing about alleged support for Hamas

A two-hour hearing in Spain’s high court Friday on the US extradition request of…

blocks.text: A two-hour hearing in Spain’s high court Friday on the US extradition request of wealthy leftwing activist and philanthropist James “Fergie” Chambers turned out to be a study in contrasts.

Chambers’s defense took most of the session to query the US citizen and detail irregularities in the Trump administration’s extradition request – several of which the Guardian has reported on – as well as the figures of Spanish law that would lead the three-judge panel to deny the request; while the prosecutor sped through his case, head down, asking Chambers no questions at all.

Notably, neither the judges or the prosecutor asked Chambers to address the insinuation in the extradition request that the wealthy activist had supported Hamas. Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money laundering charge and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

But the defense’s queries did allow him to speak for the first time since his 10 July arrest in Ibiza about events at the center of the case: 2023 protests against Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit in Massachusets and New Hampshire and 2024 transfers of $7.2m to Tunisia, where he lived at the time. The latter was buttressed with testimony from a financial expert.

On the whole, Chambers painted a picture different from the depiction contained in the extradition request, that of a violent backer of Hamas on the run from the US. At one point, he noted that his family’s next door neighbor in Tunis was the US ambassador.

The court will decide next week on extraditing Chambers. If the decision is affirmative, Spain’s council of ministers can reverse the court’s decision. This means Chambers’s extradition may be among the last decisions made under Pedro Sánchez, the socialist prime minister, before national elections on 29 November.

Friday’s hearing began with Chambers’s defense asking about his wealth. A self-described communist and anti-imperialist, Chambers sold stock back to his family’s business, Atlanta-based Cox Enterprises, worth about $250m in mid-2023.

Then he started a foundation, he told the court. He and the foundation’s three-member board decide on funding and ensure that no projects seeking support are under US sanctions, Chambers said. The foundation has funded an estimated 100 progressive and humanitarian projects in 20 countries, according to his partner, activist and actor Stella Schnabel – including, Chambers said Friday, organizations in Gaza working on issues such as “medical treatment for children, transportation out of dangerous areas and clean water and food”.
Two of the request’s three charges – riot and conspiracy to riot – are related to the late-2023 protests against Elbit.

Chambers detailed his participation in the protests: locking himself to a door, marching in the street and – in New Hampshire – standing in the road, speaking to the media and paying bail for four protesters who were eventually found guilty of misdemeanor charges and served 30 days in jail.

As for the $7.2m, the defense and a financial expert serving as a witness laid out how ten bank transfers from the US to Tunisia mostly went to sponsor the football club Club Africain – described by Chambers as “one of the largest football clubs in Africa” – and a sporting business Chambers launched while living in Tunisia.
“Is there any indication that the money went to support terrorist activities?” asked defense attorney Aitor Martínez. “None,” said financial expert Albert Deulofeu Schilt.

Then, in about 15 minutes of rapid-fire monotone, prosecutor Juan Hernández Villalba laid out a wholly different picture of Chambers as backing “an organized structure … aimed at repeatedly committing illegal acts … together with funds destined for terrorist organizations”.
He accused the defense of laying out the facts of the case “in a fragmented way … when what’s most relevant is an evaluation of the whole picture”.
“The extradition petition isn’t based on ideology or political statements, but on actions [Chambers] organized, financed and carried out, causing material damage,” Hernández Villalba asserted.
The actions against Elbit “were presented as a simple protest”, he said. “Nevertheless, the actions described by the US were planned for days … with objectively violent content.”
Given all this, the prosecutor said, “there are more than enough indications to consider … that [Chambers’s] funding was aimed at terrorism”.

Among the 100-plus people in varying time zones following Friday’s hearing on the court’s YouTube channel was Irish film-maker and journalist Sinéad O’Shea, whose documentary on Chambers called All About the Money makes its New York premiere this weekend. It covers the time period cited by the FBI affidavit underpinning the US request. O’Shea said that extradition case “builds a false narrative which begins with the protest in New Hampshire – a piece of vandalism at worst and for which people ended up serving 30 days. I saw myself the football club in which he invested in Tunisia and his donations to Palestinian and other charities are a matter of public record. It is impossible not to see this as a politically motivated case.”

Chambers’s views have been extensively profiled in US media. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
Dressed in dark jeans, a grey-blue shirt, a black jacket, with a close-cropped haircut and mustache, Chambers got the last word during the hearing.
“To this day I cannot understand why I have been in prison since July for what amounts to speaking emotionally and committing minor offenses of public disturbance,” he said.

“I’ve never had any contact with any terrorist organization. I’ve certainly never financed any terrorist organization … and for this my family has been torn apart. I missed my grandmother’s funeral last week. My five-year-old son asks where I am every day. And my wife will give birth, God willing, in March – and I don’t know if I will be by her side.”
“[All] because I have spoken my mind, and I had a lot more money than others who have spoken their mind, in my country. And that’s all it amounts to.”

articles.title: Choking fires, deadly heat and devastating floods: 2026 in extreme weather
articles.summary:
People around the world have contended with unprecedented weather events and their fatal effects caused by the climate catastrophe

After the world’s hottest summer since records began in…
articles.byline: Jonathan Watts; graphics by Sara Fiorillo

blocks.text: After the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher.

As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating, the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.
January Fourth-hottest January on record

blocks.caption: A fire in Longwood, a town in Victoria, Australia, in early January. Photograph: Michael Currie/AAP

blocks.text: Extreme heat fuels wildfires in Australia As temperatures jump nearly 20C (68F) above average, Victoria and other southern states register new heat records, including 50C in Port Augusta and the tiny opal mining town of Andamooka. Melbourne hospitals report a 25% increase in heat-related illnesses, while authorities in many areas struggle with wildfires. Scientists say the supercharged climate has made the heatwave five times more likely. Heatwaves already cause more deaths in Australia than all other natural hazards combined.
February Fourth-hottest February on record

blocks.caption: People clear mud and debris outside homes in the aftermath of a storm, in Juiz de Fora, Brazil. Photograph: Andre Coelho/EPA

blocks.text: Mudslides kill 72 in Brazil after record rain The city of Juiz de Fora in Minas Gerais records its wettest ever month, triggering landslides that sweep away hundreds of homes in poor communities on unstable hillsides. Floods also disrupt Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo. More than 10,000 people are displaced.
March Fourth-hottest March on record

blocks.caption: Motorists drive through heavy rains in the Kibera slums in Nairobi, Kenya.   Photograph: Donwilson Odhiambo/Getty Images

blocks.text: Devastating floods across much of the world In Ethiopia, at least 131 people are killed in floods and mudslides that bury entire villages. Eighty die in Kenya and 18 in Tanzania. The Arabian peninsula is battered by fierce winds and heavy downpours that flood the streets of the desert kingdom. Hailstones the size of tennis balls fall in Oman and lightning storms leave cities in the UAE inundated with water. Many areas report record rainfall. At least 30 die in Afghanistan as heavy rains trigger landslides. Hong Kong is soaked in twice the usual monthly precipitation. Flood waters in southern Russia submerge homes and leave more than 300,000 without electricity. Huge tracts of farmland are left underwater in Argentina and Chile.

World’s energy imbalance accelerates rapidly The World Meteorological Organization reveals an alarming buildup of energy in Earth’s system. More than 90% is stored in the oceans, where warming has more than doubled over the past two decades compared with the average over the previous 45 years. This makes weather more extreme and threatens health and food supplies. António Guterres, the UN secretary general, says: “The global climate is in a state of emergency. Planet Earth is being pushed beyond its limits. Every key climate indicator is flashing red.” Guterres urges the world to cut fossil fuel emissions as rapidly as possible to minimise future risks. However, CO2 in the atmosphere continues to rise.
April Second-hottest April on record

blocks.caption: A utility pole blocks a road in Saipan after a super typhoon with ferocious winds and relentless rains shredded tin roofs and forced people to take cover from flying tree limbs. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Super typhoon tears through Micronesia, Guam and Saipan At peak intensity on 12 April, Sinlaku registers a wind speed of 295km/h (183mph) – roughly the same as a Shinkansen bullet train and the joint highest recorded by a storm in the western Pacific basin so early in the year. It is also the deadliest in decades, killing 12, leaving 43,000 without power, forcing mass evacuation and causing $1.5bn (£1.1bn) in damages. This will remain one of the most powerful storms of 2026, superseded only by Super Typhoon Champi that will strike Taiwan and Japan in October.
May Second-hottest May on record

blocks.caption: A man seeks relief from the heat as temperatures rise in New Delhi, India. Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPA

blocks.text: Hundreds of millions endure deadly heat in south Asia At least 47 heat-related deaths are reported in southern Asia as temperatures soar above 45C in several Indian and Bangladeshi cities, and hit a peak of 52C in Pakistan’s southern province of Sindh. Scientists warn that the climate crisis is exposing hundreds of millions of people in south Asia to longer, deadlier pre-monsoon heat.
June Second-hottest June on record

blocks.caption: People assess the aftermath of landslides and flooding next to houses damaged in Attécoubé, a suburb of Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire. Photograph: Chris Boli/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Ocean heat enters uncharted territory Sea surface temperature graphs begin to jag upwards and away from all previous highs on 21 June, starting a trend that will worsen over the rest of the year. This alarms scientists because oceans absorb more than 90% of the excess energy in Earth’s system. If the seas start to release that heat then the land and air will get warmer more quickly. This coincides with the emergence of the latest El Niño, which is confirmed on 2 June.

Arctic and Antarctic swelter in unprecedented warmth Instead of the usual winter snow and ice, scientists at the Esperanza base on the Trinity peninsula of Antarctica are astonished to see rain and dirt outside their windows after an eight-day heatwave that peaked with a record temperature of 15C on 6 June. At the other end of the planet, the Arctic experiences its warmest ever June. Beliy Island, Siberia, registers 28.3C on 25 June, the highest temperature ever recorded that far north in the Eurasian Arctic.

West African deluge takes heavy toll Relentless rains claim almost 100 lives in west Africa from May to June. Record downpours of up to 140mm (5.5in) in a single day are made five times more likely and 23% more intense by the human-caused climate crisis. Floods and mudslides kill 59 in Côte d’Ivoire, 35 in Ghana and five in Togo.
after newsletter promotion
July Joint-hottest July on record

Fires choke Canada and Europe Almost 1,000 wildfires sweep across Canada, charring 3m hectares (7.4m acres) and sending a haze of smoke as far as New York. On 15 July Toronto registers the world’s worst air quality as a result of the haze. Smoke kills 4,000 people in Canada each year, almost four times as many as at the start of the century. Meanwhile, in Europe, prolonged droughts create tinderbox conditions for wildfires in Greece, Portugal, Italy, Norway, Germany, Spain and France. They burn 686,000 hectares in Europe, twice the average of the past 20 years.

Extreme weather disrupts US 250th birthday festivities and the World Cup Half of the US population is under a heat alert before 4 July independence celebrations, disrupting Donald Trump’s Great American State Fair on the National Mall in Washington and other events. Dozens of heat-related deaths are reported and thousands experience power cuts.
At least nine World Cup games are played in potentially dangerous heat and humidity, while fierce storms delay three matches by more than an hour, including Mexico v England.
August Hottest August on record

Nepal glacier collapse kills at least 1,300 Lhende Khola river valley communities are swept away after a 2 sq km (0.8 sq miles) slab of rock and glacier ice falls 1,400 metres (4,600ft) in the Himalayas, triggering a flood of water and debris. More than 5,000 people are missing and 8,600 need medical attention. Scientists say unusually warm temperatures and long-term permafrost degradation owing to the climate crisis were among the likely causes of the catastrophe.

Europe’s murderous heat forces reactor shutdown The UK and France are among a host of nations that swelter through the warmest summer (June to August) in European history. The heat kills an estimated 50,000 people in cities across the continent. Two-thirds of those excess deaths are attributable to the climate crisis. Many more are likely to have died in rural areas. As droughts spread, Romania is forced to shut down its only nuclear power station because the cooling system could not be replenished by low water levels in the Danube River.
September Second-hottest September on record

Record heat and deadly storms lash Asia Hundreds are killed and millions evacuated as the world’s most populous continent experiences its hottest September and severe storms. Typhoon Dujuan kills at least 10 people in Japan, with violent winds of 144km/h and 832mm of rain in only 48 hours on the island of Izu Oshima. Three die in a mudslide in eastern China during Typhoon Saudel. At least 102 are killed in India and Nepal amid rain that is nine times the norm in some places. Eight die and half a million are affected by flooding in Bangkok, Thailand.
October Hottest October on record

blocks.caption: Protesters clash with police officers in Jakarta, Indonesia, during a demonstration against President Prabowo Subianto’s handling of forest fires. Photograph: Willy Kurniawan/Reuters

blocks.text: Governments warned to brace for peak El Niño The UN disaster relief agency urges countries to prepare for an unprecedented “wrecking ball” El Niño that is forecast to peak around the end of the year. UK authorities advise households to stockpile a few days of basic supplies. Climate scientists project more than 450,000 people globally will die by February as a result of the additional heat brought by the super El Niño.

Protests in Indonesia after deadly fires Demonstrators in Jakarta protest against Indonesia’s worst fire season in a decade, which has scorched almost 2m hectares of forest – more than twice as big an area as last year. The choking haze is estimated to have killed 3,560 people in one month alone.

Roads turn to rivers in Chile After the heaviest October rainfall in 76 years, the Chilean government declares the Santiago district of Las Condes a “disaster zone”, with more than 1,000 people evacuated from their homes, some by helicopter.

Drought and fire in the Amazon rainforest Months of drought leave some of the world’s mightiest rivers, including the Rio Negro, Madeira and Tapajós, close to record low levels, curtailing the water transport of essential goods. This coincides with a sharp rise in fire activity in the central and eastern Amazon region, releasing so much smoke that the city of Manaus registers the second-worst air quality in the world on 12 October.
November

blocks.caption: Global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives. Photograph: Jesús Vargas/Getty Images

blocks.text: 2026 is forecast to be one of the hottest years in history

Global temperatures tie an all-time record of 2.04C above preindustrial levels, which was set in 2023. This year is forecast to be one of the four warmest years in history, along with 2023, 2024 and 2025. Sea surface temperatures are so high that the climate scientist Eliot Jacobson calculates the odds of being this far above the norm at 33tn to one. Meanwhile, the amount of CO2 in the atmosphere reaches a peak not seen in 2m years. On the plus side, global fossil fuel emissions are likely to fall this year thanks to a shift away from oil and gas owing to high prices after the US-Israeli attack on Iran, and ever cheaper renewable alternatives.

articles.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy says security deal could go to referendum
articles.summary: The US has broached the idea of Kyiv giving up the Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership, the Ukrainian president said.

image.caption: Zelenskyy said he could put any comprehensive security deal to a public voteImage: Francisco Seco/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said US peace envoys asked whether Kyiv would withdraw from its eastern region of ‌Donbas ⁠in exchange ⁠for joining NATO, according to remarks to the media published on Saturday.
The suggestion was made following the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi to bring Russia's nearly 5-year war in Ukraine to a close.
What did Zelenskyy say?
The Ukrainian leader told reporters: "The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would ⁠Ukraine ​withdraw from Donbas?'"

Zelenskyy repeated Kyiv's position that it was not willing to cede territory to Russia. But he added that if the country reached a comprehensive deal, including security guarantees, a ‌strong ​and well-funded Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question ​to the public in a referendum.
"That ​is why ⁠I believe NATO is back on the ⁠agenda. ​But you have also heard [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."
Zelenskyy said the prospect of NATO membership in exchange for withdrawing from Donbas has not been raised before.
He also warned about Moscow's plan to change the continent's security architecture, saying it could lead to more conflict.
Putin has demanded that NATO pull back its troops from the Russian border, which European Union leaders have strongly criticized.
"This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations," Zelenskyy added.
"Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That's it. There is no other security in Europe."
Europe chooses representatives for Ukraine peace talks
Europe to play bigger role in peace talks
On Friday, the EU said several European diplomats would take part in future Ukraine peace talks, including Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Poland.
Moscow has long insisted that European states be excluded from the negotiations because they support Ukraine.
Russian forces strike Zaporizhzhia
The comments come as Russia’s Defence Ministry said its ⁠forces ⁠had captured the ​settlement of Tersianka in ​Ukraine’s southeastern ​Zaporizhzhia ‌region, news agency Interfax reported.

Interfax cited the ministry as saying that Russian ​forces had struck Ukrainian energy and ​transport infrastructure used by ⁠the ​military, along with ammunition ​depots and ​drone production ‌and storage sites.
Russia has targeted power stations across Ukraine in waves of ballistic and cruise missile attacks, cutting power and heating to millions of people as temperatures plunge.
Zelenskyy warned that Putin was "betting everything" on this winter's war campaign, which Kyiv insists is aimed at hurting public morale.
As Russia pounds Ukraine's infrastructure, Kyiv faces winter blackouts

articles.title: Hungarian authorities uncover $20m during probe of Orbán-era minister
articles.summary: Prime Minister Péter Magyar promised a sweeping anti-corruption drive after ousting Orbán in April.

blocks.text: Nearly $20m (£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Viktor Orbán, authorities have said.

Miklós Seszták, who served as minister of national development for four of the ex-prime minister's 16-year rule, is accused of accepting bribes as part of a scheme involving the state transport company. He has denied any wrongdoing.
Hungary's new Prime Minister Péter Magyar unseated Orbán in a landslide election in April on the promise of launching a sweeping anti-corruption drive.
On Friday, following the two-day search for the cash - found in secluded locations across the country - Magyar described it as the end of the "mafia".

Investigators found wads of banknotes in safes, buried in woodlands and hidden in agricultural and residential buildings and warehouses, as part of the probe into Seszták, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) said in a statement.
The cash amounted to "5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100", it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m. It has been deposited into the Hungarian State Treasury, the body said.
The NVVH was established to investigate allegations of corruption during the Orbán rule, which Magyar has dubbed "Operation Purgatory".
Magyar promised Hungarians "regime change" during the election earlier this year and has set about undoing many Orbán-era policies since entering office.
Allegations of corruption and cronyism have long dogged Orbán, who during the course of his tenure turned Hungary into what the EU characterised as an "electoral autocracy".

articles.title: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
articles.summary: The Ukrainian president says US envoys touted the exchange as part of efforts to end the war with Russia.

blocks.text: US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The Ukrainian president's comments on Saturday come after US envoys visited Moscow and an EU summit in Dublin as part of ongoing efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance as a condition of any peace deal to deter future threats, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.
Zelensky has also consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory, despite Moscow's demands for it to cede the Donbas.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky told reporters on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow the day prior.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.
Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

There have, however, been recent signs the two can find common ground: last month, US First Lady Melania Trump was able to broker a temporary ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky to allow for evacuations and aid deliveries.
US officials had previously said that Ukrainian Nato membership was off the table.
Zelensky said on Saturday that the US proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda".
But he cautioned: "You have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.

Ceding the small portions of land Ukraine still controls there would be a small concession in practical terms, but would be symbolically significant for Kyiv because it would constitute an acceptance of the Donbas being Russian.
Zelensky has previously spoken of retaking Russian-controlled territory in four of Ukraine's regions, as well as the Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.

articles.title: This backup singer went from small-town Ontario to sharing the stage with Celine Dion, Bonnie Tyler
articles.summary: He sang with Meat Loaf, Billy Joel, Barbra Streisand, James Taylor and Air Supply. Remember that duet of Total Eclipse of the Heart with Bonnie Tyler? He sang that, too. Rory Dodd made a career out…

image.caption: Rory Dodd was just inducted into the Norfolk Music Hall of Fame. (Submitted by Rory Dodd)

blocks.text: London

He sang with Meat Loaf, Billy Joel, Barbra Streisand, James Taylor and Air Supply. Remember that duet of Total Eclipse of the Heart with Bonnie Tyler? He sang that, too. Rory Dodd made a career out of singing with the stars, and now he's being honoured in his hometown of Port Dover, Ont.
Rory Dodd is being honoured at home in the Norfolk Music Hall of Fame
He sang with Meat Loaf, Billy Joel, Barbra Streisand, James Taylor and Air Supply. Remember that duet of Total Eclipse of the Heart with Bonnie Tyler? He sang that, too.
Born and raised in Port Dover, Ont., Rory Dodd made a career out of singing with the stars. His voice is featured in some of the biggest hits of the 1970s and '80s.
Now, the life-long musician is being honoured at home as one of the latest inductees into the Norfolk Music Hall of Fame, alongside musicians Tia McGraff and Ian Bell.
Rory Dodd is one of the latest inductees into the Norfolk Music Hall of Fame. In 2022, he was also inducted into the London Music Hall of Fame in Ontario. (Forest City London Music Awards/Facebook)

"It means a great deal to receive that recognition from your hometown—to have people back home recognize that I made something of myself beyond just being the guy singing with Meat Loaf. It's a genuine honour," he said on CBC's Afternoon Drive.

"Coming from a small town of 3,200 people, it was surreal suddenly finding myself in studios with icons like Lou Reed, singing on Walk on the Wild Side, or recording with James Taylor and Carly Simon," he said.
From small-town Ontario to Broadway

Dodd's love for music started in Port Dover, where his mother worked as a music teacher. She had her children singing Irish folk songs early on, and by the time Dodd was four years old, they were singing four-part harmonies together, he said.

"I never learned to read or write sheet music, learning harmony by ear stuck with me. It shaped my ability to arrange background vocals," Dodd said. "We would listen to a track, figure out the arrangement on the spot, and record what was in my head."
It was when he travelled to New York to audition for Rockabye Hamlet on Broadway that he would make an impression on Meat Loaf , which would later launch his singing career.
Rory Dodd sings on stage with Meat Loaf. (Submitted by Rory Dodd)
"Being a harmony vocalist, I jumped in a third above him [while singing Wake Up Little Susie together]. He abruptly stopped, stating that nobody sang higher than him," he said.
Dodd replied: "Well, I do.'"

Meat Loaf then introduced him to Grammy-winning composer and record producer Jim Steinman, who sat him down at a piano to play through the forthcoming Meat Loaf album, Bat Out of Hell, which ended up being one of the greatest-selling records of all time.

"The sheer power of it blew me away, and I knew I wanted to be involved," Dodd said. "We spent a couple of years trying to land a record deal. When my visa status became an issue and I had to leave, Meat Loaf insisted I couldn't go back and offered me his couch, so I moved in with him."
Rory Dodd was a close collaborator of hitmaker and Grammy-winning music producer Jim Steinman, who featured him on many of the tracks he produced. (Submitted by Rory Dodd)
Steinman was a hitmaker and became close collaborators with Dodd.
Dodd stood out for his impressive four-and-a-half octave vocal range and an ability to pull off falsetto seamlessly, London music historian Mario Circelli said.
"He is the voice of thousands of songs you've heard, but never knew who it was," he said. "His catalogue is a who's who of what was happening in music in the '70s, '80s and '90s."
LISTEN | How Rory Dodd launched his music career:
Afternoon Drive12:03Southwest Sounds: Rory Dodd

In 1983, Dodd had backing vocals on three of the top tracks in the United States: Bonnie Tyler's Total Eclipse of the Heart, Air Supply's Make Love Out of Nothing At All and Billy Joel's Tell Her About It.
"Walking down New York streets and hearing your own voice coming out of local stores was mind-blowing," he said.
"Eventually, hearing yourself everywhere just felt like part of daily life, almost beyond full comprehension."
'The vibe is still there'
Dodd said he still performs from time to time around his hometown with his friend Mark Hukezalie, who is known for making it big in the jingle business, and also retired back home.
"We just do it when we want, and we do it for friends that we grew up with," he said.
"We're doing it just for ourselves, just because he can still play, and I can still sing, and the vibe is still there."
London is a City of Music with Mario Circelli - Rory Dodd
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Michelle Both is the producer for CBC London. She has roots in rural Ontario and holds a master's degree in journalism and communication from Western University. You can reach her at michelle.both@cbc.ca.
With files from Matt Allen

articles.title: Wolf Biermann at 90: The singer who defied East Germany
articles.summary: His life is a reflection of contemporary German history, which Biermann has addressed via his songs and sharp wit. Turning 90, he’s as feisty as ever.

image.caption: Wolf Biermann's powerful lyrics have caused political tremors — big and small — for decadesImage: Marcus Brandt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war by the River Jordan," and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

These themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's new album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he shows little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the issues shaping the world today.

In his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

blocks.caption: 'Operation Gomorrah' reduced Hamburg to rubble in 1943 and Wolf Biermann grew up — just like these children — amid the ruinsImage: dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A child caught in the Allied firestorm

This outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish. Wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

Just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly said in interviews. When the air raid sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

Yet Biermann says his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. (...) Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama."
Avenging his father

His mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann recalls. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism."

In 1953, while countless people were fleeing from East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble. He also began writing and performing his political songs.

He soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann recalls. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer."

blocks.caption: After 11 years, Biermann was thrilled to perform in front of a large audience in West Germany again in 1976Image: Sebastian Ahlers/DHM

blocks.text: Exiled from East Germany

In 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

Yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

On November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. "I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

blocks.caption: Protesting together with Green Party politicians in 1983 against the impending deportation of a Turkish dissidentImage: picture-alliance/dpa/E. Steiner

blocks.text: Protest over expulsion

In a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

"The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann writes.
'Always the same struggle for freedom'

Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he says. He became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he says. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom."

blocks.caption: Pamela and Wolf Biermann have been a couple since 1983; she is also his managerImage: Ruff/Caro/picture alliance

blocks.text: The singer-songwriter plans to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he says, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children. "I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency (dpa).

And should he ever die, he says, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. Quite a crowd, Biermann says. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
articles.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their…

image.caption: Nigeria's 2027 elections take place against the backdrop of AI-driven disinformationImage: Adekunle Ajayi/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Nigeria has just over two months to go to the polls, with incumbent President Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images, and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general elections; instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.
Is Nigeria becoming a one-party state?
Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria
Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI-use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming elections could otherwise be under attack.

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and indeed the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria finds itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online; in the run up to the 2023 elections, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates, or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

blocks.caption: Supporters of a particular candidate in the election can be manipulated easily to believe AI-driven fake newsImage: Sani Maikatanga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Artificial Intelligence: Various effects on voter behavior
Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI generated fakes are possible," says Akintunde Babatunde, Executive Director of the Abuja-based Center for Journalism, Innovation and Development (CJID)."

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.
Have some elections become an empty ritual?
Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development (CDD-West Africa), meanwhile told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into INEC's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added however that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity, but that the real threat rather lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.
"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," Mgbeahuruike said.

blocks.caption: Journalists can be just as susceptible to disinformation created by AI and other technologiesImage: Emmanuel Osodi/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Director-General of Voice of Nigeria (VON), Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.
Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech in elections
Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a new system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition; however, during the 2023 general elections, this voting process was marred by system failures of BVAS, as poor cell signal delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

blocks.caption: In Nigeria, voting procedures have increasingly been digitalized since 2011Image: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP

blocks.text: However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy:

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth; the 2023 elections recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27 percent of registered voters going to the polls.

articles.title: Turkey uses espionage accusations to pressure government critics
articles.summary: The arrest of a German foundation's employee in Istanbul this week has put the focus back on pressure tactics used by the Erdogan administration. The arrest is far from the first of its kind.

image.caption: Yonca Verdioglu Sik (at right, with her husband, journalist and MP Ahmet Sik, left) was eventually released on Tuesday evening, but her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish governmentImage: ANKA

blocks.text: When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage.

But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of the German organization, the Heinrich Böll Foundation, for whom Verdioglu Sik works. For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and women's, minority and LGBTQ+ rights.
During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now subject to a travel ban too.
Pressure on politicians

Verdioglu Sik was eventually released. Nonetheless her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. Sik is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the current government's harshest critics.

Recently Sik has been looking into a stock market scandal, which allegedly benefitted members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP, headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and their associates.
Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife.
"If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing.

Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey. Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been levelled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like non-governmental organizations and foundations.
Diplomatic disputes

Such accusations were often followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. What the many instances have in common though is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation.
In the past such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats.

For example in 2015, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet, were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin.
In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel, then working for German newspaper Die Welt, was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara.

blocks.caption: Journalist Deniz Yücel was labeled a "German agent" by Turkey's presidentImage: Bernd Elmenthaler/IMAGO IMAGES

blocks.text: Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups. Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison.
Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists.
'Hostage diplomacy'
Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, or GIGA, notes that the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years.

On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argues. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges.
"What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW.
LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey fear intensifying clampdown

Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law."
These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas observes.

For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," Tas explains. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue."

In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria, or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey.
It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas says.

blocks.caption: US pastor Andrew Brunson (center, white shirt) with his wife after his release in 2018Image: Getty Images/AFP/B. Kilic

blocks.text: Punishing process

The case of US cleric Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt.

This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already standing trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy.
In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage.
The Kavala case demonstrates this. He was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges.
But Tas says that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment."
This story was originally published in German.
No future in Turkey?

articles.title: UK-EU breakthrough will allow airport-style checks at Eurotunnel to avoid border ‘chaos’
articles.summary:
Eurotunnel owner Getlink wants to replicate ‘airport experience’ at Folkestone and Calais, without making people get out of cars

Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be…

blocks.text: Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be introduced at Eurotunnel in an attempt to prevent “short-term and long-term chaos” in Folkestone and Calais.

In a breakthrough for travellers, the European Commission has agreed to a new system in which an “eagle eye” camera system, already used in Rome and Paris airports to supervise fingerprinting and facial imaging, will be used at the border between the UK and France.
Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the Eurotunnel owner, said it had tried to replicate the “airport experience” but wanted to go much further.

Instead of getting out of the car and getting biometrics taken at a terminal building, holidaymakers and business travellers will now be greeted with special drive-through terminals in Folkestone and Calais.

blocks.caption: New airport style drive-in biometrics kiosks at Eurotunnel in Calais. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: Both sides are now equipped with 120 kiosks under the case of an eagle-eye camera that will be monitored by police, similar to e-gates at airports where police are not physically present at each gate.

In the coming weeks, Leriche will meet UK and French authorities presenting a 40-page proposal to allow Eurotunnel to become a “laboratory” for an “intelligent border” using emerging tech and lessons learned from the US and Singapore.

The entry and exit system (EES) requires all third-country citizens including British passport holders to submit fingerprints and facial images as they enter and exit the Schengen area, but has been delayed for years.
EES was supposed to be active across the EU by 9 September, but nine of the 27 EU member states, including France, have yet to be deploy it fully because of continued technical issues.

blocks.caption: The new drive-in fingerprinting terminals at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: It has always been a logistical nightmare for Eurotunnel and a potential cause of miles-long tailbacks at the approach to the terminal.

Originally, Getlink had planned to use a tablet to hand to the passengers in their cars to allow them to self-fingerprint and capture a facial image. It also looked at a system involving passengers parking up and going into the terminal to get fingerprinting.
But both models would have required the physical presence of police officers for first-time fingerprinting.

Leriche said: “We told the authorities: it is going to be a mess. Many people are going to the wrong place and you can’t have police jumping from one place to the next to solve the issues. It would also means customers would have a bad experience, particularly at peak time.
“This is not something people in airports experience, but nobody approached this before, thinking we could have an airport experience at the border here. But we said: why not?”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: He said that after “many, many discussions” with the European Commission and the French authorities, finally they were “authorised” to trial “eagle-eye cameras” at each kiosk. “The French authorities are also on board because for them it is more efficient, too, so we are all aligned on the trial,” he said.
The trial will last two years, but Eurotunnel hopes the experiment will become permanent.

Each car will be able to pull up to an individual kiosk, with two stands per vehicle to read passports and take fingerprints and facial images. “It will prevent the chaos in the long term and the short term and if the experiment works, as hopefully it will, then it will become permanent,” said Leriche.
He said the company had been inspired by visits to the US/Mexico border controls, where drivers and passengers remain in their cars.

blocks.caption: The new drive-in border controls at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian

blocks.text: The requirement of having a police officer present each time a first-time passenger, or “primo” as they are known, submits their fingerprints was designed as a safeguard against subterfuge. Criminals, for example, could use a fellow passenger for example with a “clean skin” fingerprint.

Leriche said he had no idea when the system will be introduced by France. “It has been delayed and delayed and delayed, but our kiosks are there, they are can function but the connection with the French system is still not working. It is a question was are asking all the time.”
This week it emerged that the EU had filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in the implementation of EES.

articles.title: Gen Z protests: Do Baby Boomers really have it better than young people?
articles.summary: Should young people in Germany be more worried about their future than Baby Boomers were in the 1980s and 1990s? Or should both generations take to the streets and protest together? DW checked the…

image.caption: 'It's giving anxiety about the future,' reads the sign at a Gen Z protest in Hamburg Image: Marcus Brandt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Young people across Germany and Europe are taking to the streets, voicing fears of a bleak future.
But is that really the case? Does Gen Z face greater challenges than Baby Boomers did in the 1990s? What do the two generations have in common, and where do their experiences differ?

"Of course, it's fair to ask, 'Were things just as tough for you back then?'" youth researcher Simon Schnetzer tells DW. "But young people see that things are difficult for them now, and say that's why they need support today."

Schnetzer, who wrote the annual Youth in Germany study, highlights one key question raised by the recent demonstrations across Europe as: "Have we given young people the conditions they need to live and work here with confidence, and to keep this system funded?"

His straightforward answer is no. A survey of the statistics shows that both Gen Z and the Baby Boomers are affected by major societal changes, but in different ways. DW surveyed data on pensions, education, housing and climate change to find out more.
Pensions and poverty among the elderly

The facts point to a clear trend: Fewer and fewer young people are having to support an ever-growing number of retirees. According to the Germany's public pension insurance system, there were 3.73 contributors for every retiree in 1957. By 2025, that figure had fallen to just 2.1.
By 2045, this number is projected to drop to just 1.73 contributors per retiree. In absolute terms, this means 35.35 million contributors will be financing pensions for 16.82 million retirees.

To cushion this trend and keep contribution rates stable, the pension system already receives around €118 billion [$131 billion] in annual government subsidies. This amounts to roughly 25% of the federal budget. That means an increasing share of the population will be called upon to help fund pensions.

There are also signs that many people's pensions are already falling short of covering their living expenses. The number of retirees relying on federal basic income support has risen from 257,000 in 2003 to 738,000 in 2024.
What Germans young and old think about the pension system
Rent and housing costs

Rising rents hit low-income households particularly hard. According to a report by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW), the share of income spent on rent by low-income households rose from around 24% in 1990 to nearly 36% in 2021.
This means that in 2021, the lowest-income households spent an average of 14 percentage points more of their income on rent than high-income households.
