articles.title: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
articles.summary: A new wave of youth dissent swept India this summer, fuelled by frustration and irreverent online satire.

blocks.text: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
India's Gen Z protesters are facing the limits of dissent
ByAzadeh Moshiri
South Asia Correspondent, Delhi
Cheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.
One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."

Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained.
The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire.

The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.

The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".
This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests.
But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The CJP led massive protests in July which ended with the resignation of a federal minister

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
The CJP led massive protests in July which ended with the resignation of a federal minister
"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."
The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online.
"It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations.
"The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."
Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.

In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.
Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.

Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.
His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".

blocks.caption: Image caption, The CJP in its early days became a unifier for Indian youth frustrated with the state of education, jobs and economy

blocks.text: Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Images
The CJP in its early days became a unifier for Indian youth frustrated with the state of education, jobs and economy
"We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.
Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.
Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.

CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar.
The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.
Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders.
"We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.
Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect.
"A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.
The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Tens of thousands of people gathered at Delhi's iconic Ramlila Maidan for the opposition protest on 1 November

blocks.text: Image source, Hindustan Times via Getty Image
Tens of thousands of people gathered at Delhi's iconic Ramlila Maidan for the opposition protest on 1 November
"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."
The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.
Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".
Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.
Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress.
"Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.
They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.
Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.
CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.
Yet dissent has not been stamped out.

Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities.
CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation.
When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling.
"I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."

articles.title: Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of ‘racist’ campaign against Israel’s Arab minority
articles.summary:
Statement a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis

Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier…

blocks.text: Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fuelling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab minority, after he sought to delegitimise the community’s lawmakers by linking them to Hamas.
Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis, who make up more than 20% of the population.

Two Arab-majority parties, Raam and the Joint List, secured a combined 19 seats in last month’s election, winning nearly a sixth of the 120-seat parliament and potentially emerging as kingmakers in efforts by Eisenkot to form a government.
“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” Eisenkot wrote on X on Friday.
“They have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation, fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” he added.
“The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of civic responsibility.”
Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” following its unprecedented 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis – descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948 – were also among those killed.
Netanyahu has also repeatedly alleged electoral fraud by Arab-majority parties, but electoral authorities have rejected the claims.
In a speech, Netanyahu lamented that the two Arab lists refused to recognise Israel as a Jewish state, although Raam leader Mansour Abbas has done so in the past.
He further claimed that they sought to establish either an “Islamic state” or a “nationalist Palestinian state”.
During the same ceremony, national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir heckled Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having “pledged allegiance to Hamas”.

“It is entirely legitimate to disagree with representatives of the Arab parties, even to strongly disapprove of some of them. But it is neither legitimate nor acceptable to malign an entire community, and I will not allow it,” Eisenkot said.

President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a new government on Sunday after consultations in which a majority of political parties, including the two Arab lists, recommended him for the role.
But one of Eisenkot’s rightwing allies, Avigdor Lieberman, has said he will back out of the coalition if Arab Israelis are part of it.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government within 28 days, he may request a 14-day extension. Should he still fall short, the mandate would pass to another lawmaker, most likely Netanyahu.

articles.title: Edmonton and Montreal battle for the last Grey Cup of this era
articles.summary: CBC Sports' daily newsletter previews the 113th Grey Cup game, which is the final one before the CFL introduces some controversial new rules and an expanded playoffs next year.

image.caption: CFL Most Outstanding Player Davis Alexander will lead a high-powered Montreal Alouettes offence against a stout Edmonton Elks defence in the Grey Cup. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: CFL·THE BUZZER
CBC Sports' daily newsletter previews the 113th Grey Cup game, which is the final one before the CFL introduces some controversial new rules and an expanded playoffs next year.
CFL's top two teams square off for the title before new rules arrive

One of the great traditions in Canadian sports continues on Sunday in Calgary as the Edmonton Elks and the Montreal Alouettes square off in the 113th Grey Cup. This is Montreal's third appearance in the CFL title game in four years (they won in 2023 and lost last year to Saskatchewan) while Edmonton returns for the first time since winning the Cup in 2015.

The Elks missed the playoffs in each of the past five seasons and endured a 22-game home losing streak that stretched nearly four full years before they snapped it in August 2023 (the cancellation of the 2020 season due to the COVID pandemic helped lengthen the time frame). They improved from 7-11 the last two years to a West Division-leading 13-5 with an old-school formula: run the ball, play strong defence, and win the turnover battle.

Edmonton's D did its part by allowing the fewest points and yards in the CFL while leading the league in interceptions and fumbles forced. On offence, the Elks topped the league in rushing yards with a strong running-back duo of Justin Rankin and ShunDerrick Powell and duel-threat quarterback Cody Fajardo leading the charge. The 34-year-old Fajardo threw for a career-high 4,788 yards and 25 touchdowns with an acceptable 10 picks while topping all QBs with 517 rushing yards before adding another 84 yards on the ground in last week's 28-16 playoff win over B.C.

However, sometimes the best defence is a good offence. And Montreal, which led the league in total yards gained, is favoured by a field goal this Sunday on the strength of a dynamite passing attack featuring some explosive stars.

Quarterback Davis Alexander, who was hampered by a bad hamstring in last year's Grey Cup loss, powered the Alouettes to a league-best 14-4 record and captured the CFL's Most Outstanding Player award after ranking second in the league in both passing yards and touchdowns (35) while throwing just four interceptions. He remained on top of his game in last week's 33-23 victory over Winnipeg in the East final, throwing for 372 yards and a pair of TDs.

Montreal also has an incredibly dynamic duo of receivers in Tyson Philpot and Tyler Snead, who ranked No. 1 and 2 in the league in receiving yards and each caught 13 TDs this season. Philpot, especially dangerous after he catches the ball, was named the CFL's Most Outstanding Canadian before piling up a game-high 129 yards on nine grabs in the playoff win against Winnipeg. And, just in case Edmonton didn't have enough to worry about, depth receiver Charleston Rambo went off for 117 yards on three catches against the Blue Bombers.
End of an era

This interesting matchup between the two best teams in the league should make for a good send-off in the final Grey Cup before second-year commissioner Stewart Johnston's most controversial rules changes take effect. Starting next year, the length of the field will be reduced from the CFL-signature 110 yards to the NFL standard of 100. The endzones are also shrinking, from 20 yards to 15, while the goalposts move from the goal line to the back of the endzone. The objective of all these reforms is, in Johnston's words, "trading field goals for touchdowns."

Big changes are also coming to the playoff format as eight of the league's nine teams will qualify (up from six currently) and there will be three rounds before the Grey Cup instead of two. The revamped first round even includes a pair of non-elimination games among the top two seeds in each division, who will square off for a bye to the semifinals. You can see the goal here: creating more inventory to sell to playoff-hungry broadcast partners, whose annual bill for rights fees is increasing from $50 million to about $83 million next year.
Expansion and Olympic flag news

Johnston spoke on another hot topic today during his annual state of the league address, confirming that Quebec City has emerged as a leading candidate for the CFL's long-sought 10th franchise. He said the league is talking to a prospective owner but declined to give more details.

Earlier today, the CFL and the players' union announced that they've agreed to participate in a training camp for those interested in representing Canada in flag football at the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles. It will take place from Nov. 29 to Dec. 5 in the San Diego area and 20 CFL players were invited. They include the Alouettes' Tyson Philpot and B.C. quarterback Nathan Rourke, who won the Most Outstanding Player award last year. According to the CFL, the players will "learn the rules, techniques, concepts and schemes of the international flag football game, under the guidance and evaluation of Team Canada coaches."

Flag football will make its Olympic debut at the L.A. Games, and Canada earned a spot in the men's tournament by winning the bronze-medal game at the world championships in Germany in August. The Canadian women's team also qualified before upsetting the United States to win gold.

While the CFL and its nine teams have "agreed to the parameters" of making their players available for the Olympics, it's unclear how the Canadian roster will be picked. Current members of the national team have a strong claim to be on it after their success at the worlds, and the NFL has also expressed its support for the Olympics, which could open the door for Canadian standouts like running backs Chase Brown and Chuba Hubbard to take part.

articles.title: Chaos continues for passengers stranded after U.S. airspace closed for hours

image.caption: People wait in line to rebook cancelled flights at Pearson International Airport in Toronto on Friday. (Sandra Ezekwesili/The Canadian Press)

items: November 14Few passengers, short waits at Toronto's Pearson airportHello, I'm Katie Simpson, a senior Washington correspondent with CBC News. Today I’m flying from Toronto's Pearson airport to Washington Dulles airport, as my flight is one of a few that has not yet been cancelled. Inside Pearson's Terminal 1 at the F gate, where many flights headed to the U.S. depart from, it is unusually quiet for a Saturday morning. The security process took less than five minutes, and there was no one waiting in line ahead of me to go through customs.

McCormick says he's worried there isn't robust testing of FAA system upgradesAnya ZoledziowskiU.S. officials blame now-cancelled ground stop on outdated equipment, underfundingU.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the now-cancelled national ground stop order that snarled air traffic on 'outdated equipment' and a lack of Congressional funding in what, at times, sounded like a partisan political rant against Democrats.Following the ground stop, U.S. officials blamed outdated equipment for the failure. But former FAA manager McCormick says that it's tricky to update air traffic control systems all in one go.When speaking with CBC News, McCormick, who famously shut down U.S. airspace on Sept. 11, also said that he's worried the FAA's system upgrades haven't been adequately tested. "The challenge is that trying to upgrade an air traffic control system is like trying to change the tire on a car while the car is still moving," McCormick said. "You can't just shut it down and put a new air traffic control system in its place. You have to keep the old system up and running."According to the former FAA manager, it seems a newer system overloaded an existing system, which led to the damage. That's why he's worried about whether there was robust enough testing prior to the update's integration.The FAA said in a statement it "thoroughly tested" its systems to confirm they were stable and reliable before clearing flights to resume.But don't panic; McCormick says yesterday's ground stop is a lesson learned."I'm not concerned to the point where I'm not going to fly," he said.-With files from The Associated Press

Former FAA air traffic manager says recovery will take 2 to 3 daysAnya ZoledziowskiGround stop aftermath: Why it will take days to get things back to normalCancelling the FAA ground stop order was just the first step in getting planes moving again. The National asks former FAA manager Michael McCormack to explain why it could take up to 3 days to fully restart air travel after such a major disruption.Former FAA air traffic manager Michael McCormick told CBC News that airlines will need time to sort out their operations — something that will likely take the whole weekend."You have aircraft, air crews, passenger baggage, and they're stuck in locations where they're needed elsewhere," McCormick said. "It takes time and a lot of effort to reschedule all those aircraft and air crews to be where they need to be."Airlines also have to determine which flights to delay and which ones to cancel outright, McCormick said. "Some airlines will choose to delay the flights because they need that aircraft and air crew to get to the destination airport," he said. "Other times they may choose to cancel flights because air crews may run out of their flight time and they won't be able to actually fly the aircraft."

Canadian airlines warn passengers of possible delays, cancellationsAnya ZoledziowskiPeople wait in line to rebook cancelled flights at Pearson International Airport in Toronto on Friday. (Sandra Ezekwesili/The Canadian Press)As Canadian airlines recover from yesterday's nationwide ground stop in the U.S., they're warning passengers that recovery will take some time."Schedules may continue to be impacted as operations recover," Air Canada wrote in a statement. "If your flight is impacted or if there are any changes to your itinerary, we'll notify you via email and text message."Air Canada advised passengers to monitor their flight status,WestJet meanwhile said that travellers flying to and from the U.S., Mexico or Caribbean between Friday and Sunday can make a one-time change or cancellation without penalty. But the airline warned that call centre wait times will be longer than usual.

Travellers brace for chaotic weekend after U.S. airspace shutdownAnya ZoledziowskiStranded passengers wait at Cancun International Airport after aircraft at Mexican airports with U.S.-bound flights were asked to stay on the ground on Friday. (Paola Chiomante/Reuters)This weekend will continue to be chaotic for travellers in the U.S. — and beyond. Yesterday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) suffered a communications issue in the afternoon — caused by aging and overloaded air traffic control systems, according to the White House — that catapulted the country into a nationwide airport shutdown lasting more than four hours. Thousands of flights were cancelled or delayed, including in Canada, creating chaos and uncertainty for airlines and travellers. It's only the third time the FAA has grounded flights nationwide in 25 years. The first lasted two days following the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001. And on Jan 11, 2023, the FAA paused domestic departures for some 90 minutes, also because of a communications issue.It will likely take days for U.S. flight to return to normal.

articles.title: Hungary seizes $19.5m in cash found buried in forests amid graft inquiry
articles.summary:
Anti-corruption agency carried out searches as part of investigation into Orbán-era minister accused of taking bribes

Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth…

blocks.text: Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth $19.5m (£14.8m) buried in forests and hidden elsewhere while investigating an ex-minister of nationalist former leader Viktor Orbán.

Miklós Seszták, Hungary’s minister of national development between 2014 and 2018, is accused of taking bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company, purchasing secondhand buses at inflated prices.

The prime minister, Péter Magyar, won a landslide election victory in April, ending Orbán’s 16 years in power after promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during his rival’s rule.
Seszták, two other Orbán-era ministers and the former premier’s brother have been taken into custody in different cases as graft inquiries have gathered pace in recent weeks.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), an anti-graft body with sweeping powers established as part of Magyar’s accountability drive, said it searched multiple locations on Thursday and Friday as part of the criminal proceedings against Seszták.

“During the search, investigators found large amounts of cash: buried in forests, hidden in agricultural and warehouse buildings as well as residential properties, and stored in high-value safes in secluded locations,” the statement said.
“The total amount of cash found during the two-day search was 5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and US $1,257,100,” it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m.
NVVH said its staff deposited the cash into the Hungarian State Treasury’s account.
“Upon receipt, 12 Treasury employees spent 8 hours counting the money using 5 counting machines,” finance minister András Kármán said on Facebook.
Magyar hailed the seizure as a potential turning point.
“This officially marks the end of the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” he said in reference to Orbán’s former governing coalition.
The former leader did not react to the latest development. Orbán had previously denounced the probes targeting his inner circle as “political persecution” aimed at imprisoning him.

articles.title: Watch: Cruise ship seen sinking after collision with cargo ship in New Orleans
articles.summary: All passengers have been accounted for after a cargo ship collided with a docked cruise ship.

blocks.text: A cargo ship has collided with a docked cruise ship in New Orleans, Louisiana, with reports suggesting more than 120 people were on board the cruise ship.
Eyewitness video shows the moment the cruise ship is seen sinking and the aftermath of the collision as rescue efforts are under way.
New Orleans mayor Helena Moreno has said all passengers have been accounted for.

articles.title: The dangers of revising Europe's security architecture
articles.summary: Experts warn against revising Europe's security framework because they say it would mean granting Moscow its longstanding wish of renegotiating postwar security on the continent.

image.caption: European leaders and diplomats met in Dublin to reaffirm their support for Ukraine as US-mediated peace talks gained momentum this week.Image: Virginia Mayo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: European leaders have so far found compromises in response to many of US President Donald Trump's demands.
But they were surprised to hear Trump say that he raised Europe's security framework with Russian officials.
"It's going to be a big agreement and it's going to involve more than Ukraine," Trump said after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House last week.
He said that deal might include all of Europe. But what he meant by "all of Europe" was not clear.
US envoy Jared Kushner also wrote that Europe and Russia had struggled to establish a sustainable security framework for more than 30 years.
Kushner said he was looking at a "broader" European architecture before he flew to meet with Russian and Ukrainian representatives in Abu Dhabi.

European diplomats immediately pushed back on Washington's approach to secure a peace deal in Ukraine because they feared that a peace settlement could restore Russia's sphere of influence and undermine NATO.

"We ​already have European security ​architecture in place. NATO and the European Union both have their ​respective roles. We ​must make sure Ukraine is integrated ‌into ⁠this architecture," said Kaja Kallas, the European Union's foreign policy chief.
The issue with revising Europe's postwar security framework
Russia made clear during talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week that they were keen to discuss a broader European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

"Phrases about the European security architecture are certainly Russian talking points and not only talking points but, to a degree, part of a media propaganda effort that Russia makes to frame the war as it wishes to frame the war," said Michael Kimmage, a historian of the Cold War.
Russian leaders, including Vladimir Putin, have long alleged that the US and NATO repeatedly violated pledges they made in the early 1990s not to expand the alliance into the former Soviet bloc.
They have seen NATO's enlargement during this period as having put them in a humiliating position in which they could do very little.

At the same time, in the 1990s, the European project saw the birth of the European Union, the single market that ensured the free movement of goods and people across member states, the Schengen agreement for border-free travel, and the euro.
The core idea was to extend peace across the continent.
"Europe can mean so many things, but the European project was not designed for war. It was designed for peace," said Kimmage.
During this period, there were even suggestions of Russia becoming a NATO member.
But that relative period of stability changed after Russia invaded Georgia in 2008, annexed Crimea in 2014 and launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

"Russia wants to redraw all of this by force. And I think that that's fundamentally unacceptable to Europe with all the diversity and variations that you get within the European landscape on what's acceptable and not acceptable. I think the large-scale redrawing of borders by force is just not the European project," said Kimmage.
"So to the extent that the redrawing of borders by force is the lifeblood of Russian foreign policy, and I think that's a pretty easy case to make, Russia and Europe are at an impasse," he said.
What was to happen to Ukraine's security?

The Trump administration very quickly turned to making sure that "existing European security institutions" would be intact, with Jared Kushner having said late Thursday that the next round of negotiations would include "our European partners."
Kushner, along with Steve Witkoff, flew to Moscow to talk to Putin after talks in Abu Dhabi. Then they flew to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Kushner had earlier Thursday signaled some "really incredible" postwar plans for Ukraine, saying that it could not be concluded without Europeans at the table.

"We should not allow a diktat from Russia that would result in some kind of neutralization or significant reduction in the military forces of Ukraine going forward, because that would make Ukraine very, very vulnerable to future aggression and pressure coming from Russia," said Hiski Haukkala, the director of the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.
That would mean that Ukraine would also be completely dependent on the security guarantees that the US or Europeans are able and willing to provide.

"We are supporting Ukraine because we are supporting international law and the basic norms of decency and international security when it comes to European security architecture. And this is the vantage point from which we are operating," he said.
The European Union has repeatedly pointed to some of the basic treaties that Russia broke, including:

items: The UN Charter
The Helsinki Act of 1975, which established the ten core principles of European security, including the non-use of force or threat against territorial integrity.
The Charter of Paris for a New Europe that built on Helsinki commitments
The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), which was one of the few multilateral security forums where the West and Russia engaged.
The Budapest Memorandum of 1994 in which Russia, the US and the UK provided security assurances to Ukraine and others in exchange for them giving up their nuclear weapons.

blocks.text: "Russia walked away from these principles and smashed them to pieces in the process. And they are not interested in reinstating the previous security architecture order. They want something different in its stead. And as long as this is not on the table, the Russian form of negotiation is to wage war. War is a form of bargaining," Haukkala said.
"And they are signaling strategic intent to change the makeup of European security, to subdue Ukraine and to change the very essence of European security," he added.

blocks.caption: US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Volodymyr Zelenskyy after having met Vladimir Putin in Moscow.Image: Peter Morrison/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What is the way forward?
Daniel Fried, a former assistant secretary of state for European Affairs in the George W. Bush administration, said Russia is very good at sticking to its demands.
He said Russians know how to negotiate and "right now, they are not negotiating," referring to talks in Abu Dhabi.
Some experts said there was no possibility of having a new security architecture with the Russians at this point because there was no trust or common vision to align with Russia at the moment.
Others like Balazs Jarabik, an expert on post-Soviet politics, said that Russia was part of the European security architecture whether Europeans liked it or not.

"And the question is whether it's included as our enemy. Obviously, Russia is not going to be a partner, right? We have to find a modus operandi to reduce the risk of a horizontal escalation and potentially a bigger European war, even a bigger one than what we have now."

A host of European leaders on Friday rejected the Russian demands to discuss Europe's security framework as well, with a spokesperson for the German government saying that Berlin was looking to host a meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" to secure funding for Ukraine's defense and reach a unified position regarding future peace talks.
Can Germany make Europe pay more for Ukraine?

articles.title: Watch: Divers explore US ship sunk off Florida coast to create new reef
articles.summary: The ship was intentionally sunk off the coast of Florida in order to create the world's largest artificial ocean reef.

blocks.text: The ship, which was once the fastest in the world and longer than the Titanic, was intentionally sunk off the coast of Florida, in order to create the world's largest artificial ocean reef.
The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will become a home for sea life and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.
Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila
articles.summary: Leaders and representatives of the 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, and their allies, are gathering in Manila for the bloc's biggest event of the year

blocks.text: The global energy crisis, food security, and transnational crime are among the top issues on the table as Southeast Asian leaders and their allies converge in Manila.
The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations for 2026, is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from Sunday, November 15, to Tuesday, November 17.

Aside from leaders and representatives of ASEAN’s 11 members, other world leaders will be in attendance, including United States President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and newly reelected Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is embarking on a state visit to the Philippines before the summit.
During the summit’s closing ceremony, the Philippines will also turn over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore, which will lead the bloc in 2027.

Check out this page for the latest ASEAN Summit news, photos, videos, and insights. For more updates and to share your own views, you can also join the Security and Global Affairs chat room in Rappler’s Muni app.

articles.title: Iran says it destroyed US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike
articles.summary:
First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and…

blocks.text: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain – its first direct attack on US military installations for months – in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz.

“This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.”

Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes.
Trump announced that he had asked his vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states.

Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal.

Vance has been in the forefront of Republicans saying the war led to the massive Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public, since higher diesel prices was a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

An opinion poll in the UK shows 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu).
It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was found to be 45%, with 22% opposed.

The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda.

Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.”

Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon.

In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for reviewing Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”.

The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning.

Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely inside political and security circles.
Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested.

The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”

articles.title: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
articles.summary:
Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week,…
articles.byline: Ed Walton and Alice Nightingale-Smith for MetDesk

blocks.text: Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm in 12 hours. Lisbon saw 183 flights cancelled on Wednesday, around a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.

After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.

blocks.caption: Waves crash into a fort near Estoril as Storm Charles hits mainland Portugal. Photograph: Zed Jameson/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.

Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.

Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.

A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.
after newsletter promotion

articles.title: Nvidia scandal sparks US national security furore and calls to take tough line on China
articles.summary: Former CEO Jensen Huang and US commerce secretary to appear before Congress amid bipartisan concern that America’s security was put at risk

blocks.text: Nvidia’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang and Donald Trump’s commerce secretary are expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks, as the fallout from Huang’s reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy reverberated across the US, sparking bipartisan concerns for national security and calls for a tougher stance against Beijing.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Huang and Nvidia must answer as to whether America’s security had been jeopardised, adding that the Trump administration also must account for what it did once it learned about Huang’s reported relationship with Alice Huang, who is accused of spying for China.

Donald Trump’s close ties with Jensen Huang have also come under renewed scrutiny as a timeline of the saga started to emerge. The president called Jensen Huang two days before he stepped down and urged him to fight for his job, the New York Times has reported.

On Thursday, Schumer questioned what Donald Trump knew when he personally invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, adding: “Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.”
House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said he had demanded a classified briefing for all members of Congress about Nvidia.

The scandal has also drawn in Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, after criticism of his department’s oversight of Nvidia’s exports to China and its refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist.
“Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the banking committee to address their questions,” Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News.

Republican Tim Scott, the Senate banking committee chair said he had sent letters asking Lutnick and Jensen Huang to appear before him because: “Recent reports raise serious ‌concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology.”
Scott said he would consider subpoenaing Huang if he did not voluntarily appear. “The American people deserve answers,” Scott said.

Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday, and was replaced on an interim basis by chief financial officer Colette Kress after reports emerged of multiple affairs, key among them with Alice Huang, who is no relation but is suspected to be a Chinese spy.

The statement from Nvidia’s board of directors confirming Huang’s departure did not mention the spying scandal and personal conduct revelations, instead paying tribute to Huang’s “profound” contributions to the company he co-founded.
House foreign affairs chair Brian Mast, a Republican, said on Thursday that congressional staff had spoken to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Jensen Huang’s testimony.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was now growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China.

Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against ​China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to ‌limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does ‌not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson told reporters ‌at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.“

Chinese AI companies are now trying to secure Nvidia chip capacity outside China, amid growing concern that the gap in US export controls may now be closed after the scandal, people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
Beijing has also stepped up efforts to develop domestic alternatives, including through Huawei, although analysts say Chinese chips remain less efficient for training advanced AI models.
Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements issued since Monday.
On Chinese social media, many expressed surprise at what they see as the swift resignation, and mourned the sudden end of an era that lasted for over three decades.
News of his resignation attracted more than 400m posts overnight on Chinese microblogging platform Weibo.

Huang had enjoyed rock-star status in China, where his visits drew crowds seeking selfies and autographs and his casual outings became social-media sensations. During a January 2026 visit, opportunistic sellers advertised photographs with him for 25,000 yuan ($3,700), while a Beijing restaurant launched a special menu costing more than 400 yuan after he ate there.
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li

articles.title: Boxer on death row in Iran vows ‘not to bow before oppression’ after winning rights prize
articles.summary:
Political prisoner Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran, given prestigious Magnitsky humanitarian award

A boxer and political prisoner on death row…

blocks.text: A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”.

Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, an Iranian boxing champion, coach and political prisoner, has been sentenced to death three times and is one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran. He was given the Magnitsky award for outstanding human rights activist at a ceremony in London on Thursday night.

In a written message from Vakilabad prison in north-eastern Iran, he said: “I accept this award in the name of all those who, for the ‘crime’ of aspiring to a free Iran, have been imprisoned, tortured, threatened, or sentenced to death; in the name of my comrades in the resistance units and the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives.”
He added: “The regime demands repentance, televised confessions and surrender from us. But our answer is clear: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’”

blocks.caption: Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’ Photograph: Iran Human Rights

blocks.text: Vafaei Sani, 31, was arrested in 2020 for taking part in nationwide democracy protests in 2019 and accused of supporting an opposition group, the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK).

He was convicted of “corruption on Earth” and sentenced to death for a third time in September 2024 after “a grossly unfair trial”, according to Amnesty International. The supreme court upheld his death sentence on 4 October 2025. Since his arrest he has been tortured and held in solitary confinement for extended periods.

His continued imprisonment has drawn widespread international condemnation from prominent sportspeople, human rights organisations and legal experts who have called for his immediate release and the annulment of his death sentence.

The Magnitsky awards are named after the Russian lawyer, Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody after exposing government corruption. They began in 2015 as a way to recognise journalists, politicians and activists in the field of human rights.

Sir William Browder, head of the Magnitsky Justice Foundation and the chair of the awards committee, said Vafaei Sani’s case was emblematic of the plight of many Iranians who face execution for standing against the regime. “Most important, Mohammad Javad is still alive,” he said. “That is why this award matters. Every time the world pays attention, it becomes harder to kill him quietly.”

blocks.caption: The awards are named after lawyer Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody. Photograph: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP

blocks.text: According to the Hengaw Organisation for Human Rights, at least 710 people have been executed in Iran since the beginning of 2026, including 79 political and religious prisoners.

In an October report, the organisation documented at least 106 death sentences against January protest detainees, 35 of whom had already been executed. In Vakilabad prison, where Vafaei Sani is detained, five people have been executed linked to the protests and 15 others are facing death sentences.

Vafaei Sani’s award comes at a time when there are growing fears for imprisoned Iranian athletes, who are considered role models in the country. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, founder of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The situation is really dire … We have seven athletes at risk of execution now, including Vafaei Sani.”

Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a mountaineer, was executed on 14 October after the anti-government protests. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, earlier that month, and the mixed martial arts fighter Gholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hanged in May.

Abdollahkhani said people had been celebrating Vafaei Sani’s award. “Even people who don’t support his political view are supporting him to be heard,” she said. “I find it very inspiring that different political groups are coming together to say no to execution.”

In his message, Vafaei Sani said he wanted “a free and democratic Iran … where the people vote freely, women and men are equal, there is no discrimination on the basis of ethnicity, religion or belief, and no one is imprisoned or executed for political opposition”.
He added: “I remain steadfast in my pledge, and I will not bow before oppression until the people of Iran are free.”

articles.title: Teen prodigy, Netflix star, prisoner: the story of Hong Kong dissident Joshua Wong – podcast
articles.summary: Pro-democracy activist Nathan Law and journalist Danny Vincent on the sentencing of the iconic Hong Kong campaigner Joshua Wong to another 10 years in prison.…
articles.byline: Presented by Helen Pidd with Danny Vincent and Nathan Law; produced by Guy Szafman and Brian McNamara; executive producers Sami Kent and Alex Atack

blocks.text: He has been leading protests since he was 14. Joshua Wong has been on the cover of Time magazine, the focus of a Netflix documentary and an icon for Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement.
Wong has been leading the fight against a Chinese squeeze on freedoms in Hong Kong for the last 15 years. He will now spend more than 16 years in prison.
As Danny Vincent explains, the 30-year-old was sentenced last week to a further 10 years in prison, convicted under the island’s draconian national security law.
Helen Pidd also hears from Joshua’s friend – and fellow movement leader – Nathan Law about the prospects for democracy in Hong Kong.

articles.title: Two men found guilty of helping Iran try to ‘eliminate’ UK-based journalists
articles.summary:
Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on targets

Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a…

blocks.text: Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of assisting Tehran’s intelligence services.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.

These subjects included two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner.

The defendants visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They appear to be part of a growing new tactic used by hostile states in which “proxies” are hired to work for foreign security forces, with often little idea who they are targeting or why.

Last month the Norwegian teenager Johannes Natland, 19, was jailed for life after he agreed to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.
The Iranian men came to the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022 – Sepahvand in the back of a lorry and Manesh in a small boat.

Sepahvand used the AI platform ChatGPT to find the home address of Pourmohsen, who worked for the London-based Persian language broadcaster Iran International. He hoped to be paid £150,000 to carry out a violent attack and help to “finish off” Pourmohsen.
Sepahvand chatted on WhatsApp to his handler, an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander called Amin, as he spied on Pourmohsen in December 2024, Woolwich crown court heard.
Amin wrote: “These are new pictures of the guy/bloke.”
Sepahvand replied: “I’ll go tomorrow.”
Referring to a picture, Amin said: “And that dot is their office?”
Sepahvand said: “Love you brother, I’ll go there tomorrow.”
The pair also discussed surveillance of the Iranian satirist Kambiz Hosseini, who eventually had to leave home because of the threats made against him.

blocks.caption: Court artist sketches of (L-R) Shapoor Noori, who was  cleared of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct, Sepahvand and Manesh. Illustration: Elizabeth Cook/PA

blocks.text: Bill Emlyn Jones KC, prosecuting, said Iran and its rulers did not and could not tolerate dissent. “One organisation critical to the regime, and therefore very much in its sights, is Iran International, a news organisation which has come under particular attack because of its explicit support for opposition groups and its editorial stance, which is anti-Islamic Republic of Iran.
“Eliminating hostile, critical or dissident actors overseas is a staple policy of the Islamic republic. Together, the defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying,” Jones said.

Hosseini, 51, had to leave home and stop work as a standup comedian as a result of the threats he received. He was sent a message with a picture of his car saying the next time he started the engine it would blow up. Hosseini’s family in Iran also received threats, and his family had to leave the country.
The court heard Sepahvand had been convicted of theft in Iran and was drawn into the plan to “eliminate” dissidents in the hope of reducing his criminal record.
after newsletter promotion
He told his Iranian handlers he was prepared to escalate from surveillance to violence, the court heard.

He hoped to receive a final payment of £150,000 for “finishing the job”, a reference to killing one of the journalists, the court was told. “If the person [the target] is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him off,” said Sepahvand in a voice note.
Sepahvand claimed his family was being threatened and that he never intended to go through with the hit. He also denied plotting to kill Turner.
Manesh claimed he took a picture of the Iran International site because it was “a beautiful building” and did not know they were working with the Iranian intelligence services.

Earlier this year, Roman Lavrynovych, 22, and Stanislav Carpiuc, 27, were jailed at the Old Bailey for seven and two years respectively for arson attacks on property connected to Keir Starmer. An anonymous Russian-speaking figure named El Money had recruited Lavrynovych and Carpiuc on Telegram.

Last year, six Britons were jailed for their parts in a Russian-ordered arson attack on a London warehouse providing aid to Ukraine. The ringleader, Dylan Earl, was recruited by the Wagner group, a mercenary organisation that acts on behalf of the Russian state.

Sepahvand was convicted by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct. Manesh was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service, but cleared of preparatory conduct.
Shapoor Noori, 57, of Ealing, was cleared by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.
Sepahvand, Manesh and Noori had claimed asylum in the UK and received temporary leave to remain. None of them had regular full-time employment.
It is understood they met by chance and were then directed by Sepahvand and his contacts in Iran. There appeared to be no evidence of any wider plot.
Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded Sepahvand and Manesh before sentencing at the Old Bailey on 17 December.
